news_communities.title: Discover Chelsea Car Show & Marketplace Daws Community to Chelsea Square
news_communities.author: Record Staff
news_communities.summary:
Special to the Record

The Chelsea Chamber of Commerce, in partnership with the City of Chelsea, hosted a Car Show and Marketplace on Saturday, July 25, from 2:00 p.m. to 6:00 p.m. at Chelsea Square. The event provided local vendors, businesses, and nonprofit organizations with an opportunity to connect with residents while attendees explored a variety of classic and customized vehicles from Chelsea and neighboring communities. The Car Show and Marketplace is also part of the “Summer at the Square” event series, which brings free entertainment and family-friendly activities to Chelsea residents throughout the summer.

Residents had the opportunity to shop from a variety of local vendors offering food, jewelry, and other goods while learning about community resources from participating organizations. Businesses participating this year included Bella Isla, Orlando’s Fully Bakery, John’s Pizza, Koffee Glow, Detalles que Enamoran, Changing Seasons Creations, Cinco de Mayo, and Tacos las Toxicas. Chelsea Pride Youth Sports and the Massachusetts Department of Children and Families (DCF) Foster Care program also hosted informational tables to share resources with attendees.

More than 25 vehicles competed for awards, including first, second, and third place, Best in Show, and Best Motorcycle. The competition featured a wide range of vehicles, from Honda Civics and Corvettes to a Pontiac Catalina. Third place was awarded to Jose Baez and his Cadillac, second place to Sergio Lara and his Ford Thunderbolt, and first place to David Rizzuto and his Pontiac Catalina. Best in Show was awarded to Viny Hernandez for his Honda Civic. Winners were selected by volunteer judges Armando Montes (Montes Jewelry), Charlie Guiffrida (City of Chelsea), and Bernabe Rodriguez (City of Chelsea).

Before the awards were presented, attendees observed a moment of silence in honor of Erik Vega of Skymile Towing, who passed away last year. Vega was remembered as someone who was “always willing to lend a helping hand, especially when it came to his hometown of Chelsea, Massachusetts.”

The Chelsea Fire Department and Chelsea Police Department also participated in the event. The Fire Department displayed one of its fire engines for residents and families to explore, while the Police Department handed out ice cream to attendees. Captain Thomas McLain Jr. loaned his fully restored, vintage to participate during the event.

Entertainment was provided by DJ and the salsa band Remembranza, creating a lively atmosphere throughout the afternoon. “The annual Car Show and Marketplace reflects what makes Chelsea such a vibrant community,” said Jennifer Hassell, Executive Director of the Chelsea Chamber of Commerce. “By bringing together local businesses, nonprofit organizations, and residents, we’re creating opportunities to support our local economy while celebrating the people and partnerships that make Chelsea unique.”

The Chelsea Chamber of Commerce looks forward to continuing to partner with the City of Chelsea to host community events that support local businesses, foster community engagement, and create opportunities for residents to connect throughout the year.

The Chelsea Chamber of Commerce is committed to the economic prosperity of Chelsea’s business community by assisting, training, connecting, and advocating for businesses, organizations, and residents to help the community thrive.

news_communities.title: Richard Katz
news_communities.author: Record Staff
news_communities.summary:
Chelsea has lost a long-time member of our business community with the passing of Richard Katz, who was the proprietor of the legendary Katz’s Bagels for more than 50 years.

Katz (pronounced Kates) took over the business in the early 1970s from his father Harry, an emigrant from Russia who opened the bakery in 1938. Richad was born and raised in Chelsea, where he was an outstanding basketball player, before his family moved to Marblehead in 1957.

Under Richard’s ownership, Katz’s Bagels became a mecca for generations of Chelsea residents, many of whom continued to make the pilgrimage to the little shop in the unique triangular building at Congress Ave. and Park St. long after they had left the city in order to bring home a taste of Chelsea from their youth.

For our part, whenever our family members flew in for the holidays, we made sure to bring a dozen of Katz’s bagels to welcome them.

Katz introduced innovations such as the ever-popular pizza bagel and the bagel dog, which were treats for those of us who worked late at night or wanted a bite to eat after a night out in Boston.

In its own way, Katz’s was the Cheers (from the TV show) of Chelsea, a place where everyone knew your name and no matter the time of day, you would run into someone you knew.

Richard Katz worked long hours, seemingly around the clock, but always was a friendly-face to greet his customers.

We know we join with all of our fellow residents and long-time customers in offering our condolences to his family. May he rest in peace.

news_communities.title: Mayor Nicholson empowering youth success
news_communities.author: Olivia HaydarOlivia HaydarOlivia Haydar
news_communities.summary:
LYNN — To support young adults working to make a difference in the community, Mayor Jared C. Nicholson requested that all youth workers take part in a workshop to help prepare them for their futures. 

Nicholson’s Youth Summer Employment program focuses on putting 16- to 21-year-olds in jobs throughout the community, strengthening the level of positivity in Lynn. The program has been active for years, and this year marks the third workshop, according to Program Coordinator Allison Perry. 

“This workshop is to teach the kids financial literacy, career development, and then through the Public Health Department we have mental health and we have an opioid working group that’s going to come and talk to them as well,” Perry said. 

Out of the 350 young adults that are under payroll for this year’s youth program, more than 205 showed up for the five-hour workshop at City Hall on Wednesday to learn more about bettering their own lives in addition to their own communities. 

With social media becoming more and more likely to spread misinformation that leads youth into a downward spiral about their futures, Perry believes this workshop is imperative to provide them not only a place to go with questions, but also information they can use for the rest of their adult years. 

The first workshop, held by Eric Díaz, the assistant vice president and community and partnership development specialist at Eastern Bank, shared how the youth workers can make money their friend rather than foe. 

Díaz explained the difference between fiscal needs and wants, the difference between fixed, variable, and discretionary expenses, and even how to manage credit card balances to maintain good credit, impacting future home buying. It all starts with keeping track of your expenses, Díaz said. 

“Oftentimes you sit there, and you don’t really realize how much money goes out the door. You don’t realize that getting Starbucks every morning and getting that $8 matcha latte over five days, over a month, over a year, that’s a couple thousand dollars,” Díaz said. “That’s the reality.” 

The combination of doing a financial literacy workshop that led into a mental health workshop was intentional, Sydney Denham, Administrative and Financial Coordinator with the Department of Economic and Community Development, said. 

Denham shared that it’s a versatile spectrum of experiences that the youth workers have, and making mental health activities and terminology aware to them can open up doors to being able to communicate about struggles they have. 

“There’s a wide array of what their support at home looks like, and I think having these speakers bring their knowledge and wisdom for people that are out in the field doing these things is just really important to show them where they can go (in their futures).” 

The experiences in the youth employment program have led to full-time positions in city departments, Perry said; however, they do not stop there. They even create lasting friendships that move into university. 

“We’ve seen crew members work together over the summer and then become college roommates,” Denham said. “It builds friendships just as much as it builds that work experience, and they were roommates all throughout college, and now are best friends.”

news_communities.title: Editorial: What John Fetterman forgot about his U.S. Senate seat
news_communities.author: Guest EditorialGuest EditorialGuest Editorial
news_communities.summary:
Editorial written by The Philadelphia Inquirer Editorial Board

Pennsylvanians were well acquainted with John Fetterman’s idiosyncrasies by the time he was elected to the U.S. Senate four years ago. No one had a right, for example, to expect him to report for Capitol Hill duty with a clean shave and a pressed suit.

His supporters do deserve to be dismayed, however, at their increasingly right-leaning senior senator’s self-indulgent recent threats to leave the Democratic Party entirely. Fetterman won a competitive race as a Democrat thanks to voters who believed in him and his politics even after a stroke forced him off the campaign trail for months. If they wanted a Republican senator, they could have voted for the crudité-shopping TV doctor Fetterman was running against, Mehmet Oz.

For a man who styles himself as such a Washington outsider that he can barely be bothered to put on a pair of long pants, Fetterman is making a very inside-the-Beltway mistake. Judging by his willingness to change his positions and party at a whim, he seems to think the Senate seat belongs to him rather than the people he represents.

After nearly half the Democrats in the House voted against aid to Israel recently, Fetterman said he would leave the party should it incorporate such opposition into its platform and “officially become the anti-Israel party.” That makes his inconstancy sound more high-minded than it really is.

While the vote represented a high-water mark of Democratic opposition to Benjamin Netanyahu’s government and its wars in Gaza and Lebanon, there is no sign Fetterman suddenly finds himself in a party that believes Israel “doesn’t deserve to exist,” as the senator put it. Nearly 100 Democratic representatives took the pro-Israel side of the same vote, after all.

Nor is this some inexplicable or unforeseeable about-face on the part of Fetterman’s fellow Democrats in Congress. The party’s lawmakers are only beginning to catch up with public dismay at the conduct of Israel’s hard-right regime. One recent poll found that about a third of American adults, including a similar share of Jewish Americans and half of Democrats, believe Israeli forces committed genocide in Gaza.

The Netanyahu government, which launched its campaign against Hamas in Gaza after the horrific terror attacks of Oct. 7, 2023, has vociferously deflected that suggestion. In a statement last week, the prime minister’s office said that “Israel has taken unprecedented wartime measures to minimize harm to civilians while confronting Hamas, a genocidal terrorist organization that uses Palestinians as human shields and deliberately targets innocent Israeli civilians.”

Even if Fetterman’s stated pro-Israel principles are accepted at face value, moreover, they don’t account for the extent of his ideological migration. Perhaps his defense of Israel can be stretched to explain his avid and anomalous support for President Donald Trump’s unpopular and unsuccessful war in Iran.

But the senator has also voted for Republican measures to fund Trump’s immigration crackdown, supported his billion-dollar ballroom, objected to fewer cabinet nominees than any other Democrat, and signed off on one of Trump’s judicial nominations, the first in his caucus to do so this term. (Despite backing those initiatives, Fetterman says that his internal metrics show he votes with his party 93% of the time.)

He has also become a Fox News fixture who has accused the Democratic base — the people who, you know, gave him his job — of being “anti-American.” No wonder he is polling better among the state’s Republicans than the GOP’s own senator from Pennsylvania, Dave McCormick.

Despite Fetterman’s proclaimed “moral clarity” on Israel, he often speaks of his grievances with his fellow partisans — and his appreciation for Trump — in political rather than policy terms. He has groused about the repercussions of left-leaning Democrats’ positions for swing-state politicians like him, enthused about Trump’s sheer political talent, and lamented the electoral fate of Democrat Bob Casey, his former Senate colleague.

Maybe the senator’s red shift is motivated less by foreign policy than by an impulse to keep his job — even if it means betraying his voters. In that case, he should at least do his former supporters the courtesy of refraining from dressing up his careerism as morality.

news_communities.title: Commentary: Wonder why the birthrate is falling? Look how we treat mothers.
news_communities.author: Guest CommentaryGuest CommentaryGuest Commentary
news_communities.summary:
Christine Michel Carter

If I were deciding today whether to become a mother, I would say no.

That is something that I, as a mother, am not supposed to admit. It sounds ungrateful, as though I must immediately explain how much I love my children.

So let me be clear: My children have made me better, softer, sharper, fiercer and more alive. They are not the problem. The problem is what this country asks of mothers — and how little it offers in return.

The latest provisional data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention show that U.S. births fell 1% in 2025 and that the general fertility rate has declined since 2007. The usual response is to ask why people are not having more children. I think the harder question is why we keep asking women to enter motherhood under conditions that so many mothers describe as punishing.

When I became pregnant with my first child, I was young and hopeful. Then my daughter was born at 31 weeks and one day. Motherhood began for me in a neonatal intensive care unit, visiting a baby I could not bring home.

The Family and Medical Leave Act protected my job, but it did not protect my income. That distinction sounds bureaucratic until it is your body, your baby, and your bank account. While I was trying to understand what was happening to my daughter, I was also trying to prevent a financial disaster. A few weeks after giving birth, I went back to work.

That experience shaped years of advocacy. I wrote about pregnancy discrimination, pumping at work, Black maternal mortality and the economic penalty women pay for doing the labor this country claims to value. I spoke with lawmakers and worked in spaces where motherhood was translated into employment policy, public health, legal protection and legislative change.

For years, I believed that if mothers brought enough data, testimony and moral clarity, the country might finally become honest about what it owes us.

Then the pandemic made the hidden bargain impossible to ignore. Schools closed. Child care collapsed. Work continued. Families absorbed the shock, and parents — especially mothers — were often expected to keep performing as workers while replacing the systems that had disappeared around them.

The country called us resilient, which is often what it calls women when it does not intend to repair the conditions that are exhausting them.

Now, when women say they do not want children, I do not tell them they will change their minds. I understand them.

Not every woman who does not want children is making an economic or political statement. Some simply do not want to become mothers, and that choice requires no defense. But a country that worries about declining birth rates cannot dismiss the material conditions under which women are expected to give birth, recover, earn money, and raise children.

The American workplace is still organized around an ideal worker who has no body, no children, no aging parents, no illness, no grief and no caregiving responsibilities. Motherhood exposes that fiction. Instead of rebuilding work around the reality of human lives to support all parents and other caregivers, we keep asking families to contort themselves around it.

No employer has to order a mother back to work before she has healed when the system has already made rest unaffordable. Unpaid leave says it. Rent says it. Health insurance says it. Student loans say it. Child-care bills say it. The professional expectation that she remain available, grateful and composed says it.

When women ask for the basic infrastructure that would make raising children more sustainable — paid leave, affordable child care, maternal healthcare and wages that can support a family — children are treated as a private lifestyle choice. Yet when politicians discuss falling birthrates, family values or the future workforce, motherhood suddenly becomes a national concern — and politicians dwell on how to encourage more Americans to have more babies. Where is the support for people who are already parenting? That would send a powerful message. Instead, according to the Department of Labor, in some counties care for one child can cost more than rent. That also sends a message.

America does not love mothers as much as it loves the story of mothers: the baby bump, the gender reveal, the Mother’s Day brunch, the campaign photo of a politician holding a baby. It loves us most when our sacrifices are quiet — our bodies, our income, our sleep, our mental health, our careers.

Women considering motherhood are reading the fine print. Have the baby, but do not complain about the cost. Have the baby, but do not expect paid leave. Have the baby, but child care is your problem. Have the baby, but do not let motherhood affect your performance. Have the baby, but if the school calls at 11 a.m., somehow be both a fully available worker and a fully available parent.

I respect women who understand that not having a child may be an act of self-preservation. I refuse to lie to them. I have spent too much of my professional life asking America to value mothers and too much of my personal life learning how often it does not.

Paid leave is not a perk. Child care is not a personal indulgence. Maternal health is not a niche issue. These are conditions that determine whether families can move through ordinary life, let alone crisis, without collapsing.

Motherhood has given me more than I can explain. It has also taken more from me than this country is willing to admit. Both things can be true. I can love my children and still say I would not choose this path again. I can honor motherhood without recruiting other women into a broken system.

Before asking why women are choosing not to have children, America should ask whether it has done enough to deserve their motherhood.

Christine Michel Carter is a writer and maternal activist.

news_communities.title: Saugus’ Rooney still kicking at 83
news_communities.author: Elizabeth Della PianaElizabeth Della PianaElizabeth Della Piana
news_communities.summary:
SAUGUS — When 83-year-old Saugus resient Virginia “Ginnie” Rooney dropped her grandson off at Sun Taekwondo Academy in Danvers, she never thought she’d be getting on the mat, let alone earning a 2nd-degree black belt.

“I sat there 45 minutes every class twice a week watching him. And he was really good. Master (Soon Woo) Hong had him doing splits against the wall. And they had a Christmas party and said they were looking for people for Mom’s Club,” Rooney said.

Rooney had recently turned 70, and after inquiring about whether Master Hong thought she could do it, she was told: “You’re never going to know unless you try.” Rooney showed up on Saturday, and the rest is history.

“I threw up after every class for the first month. I really did. But then it was like, ‘Oh my God, I can do things,'” she said.

At 75, Rooney decided to try out Taekwondo and fell in love with the sport.

Despite the difficulties, she continued to move forward, earning her belts and reaching a 2nd-degree black belt this year.

When asked what her favorite thing to do was, she enthusiastically said breaking boards, and even broke a 1-inch board with an axe kick to show her skills.

“Being here gives me energy. I’ll be 84 in December. I don’t want to stop. The only time I miss a class is if I’m really sick in bed. I think I’ve missed maybe three classes in eight years,” Rooney said.

She said the best thing the classes have taught her is how to stand up straight, adding that they teach you how to fully throw your shoulders back and keep good posture.

Rooney said that her husband and son had been against her taking Taekwondo lessons, but she looked at them and told them, “I don’t care.”

Rooney was grateful for Master Hong, Master Ray Muldoon, and fellow 2nd-degree black belt Ivy Muldoon for helping her achieve her 2nd-degree black belt.

She joked that she hasn’t been able to convince any of her friends to join the class, saying that she has tried in the past but was turned down every time.

“If you don’t put your foot forward, you’re never going to get anywhere. And that’s it. If you don’t try, you’re never going to succeed,” Rooney said.

She said that she plans to continue doing Taekwondo until her body and doctor won’t let her anymore.

“My doctor thinks it’s the best thing I ever did for my body. I can do more now than I ever could. … Yes, it’s very physical, but it’s also very spiritually based. It’s a full body experience,” she said.

news_communities.title: Peabody man, 34, arrested for child porn
news_communities.author: Amanda LureyAmanda LureyAmanda Lurey
news_communities.summary:
PEABODY — A Peabody man has been arrested and charged with allegedly transporting child pornography after authorities discovered child sexual abuse material on his cellphone during an inspection at Boston Logan International Airport.

Felix Santos, 34, was charged by criminal complaint with one count of transporting child pornography. He was arrested and appeared in court in Boston on Tuesday.

Court documents state that Santos was referred to a secondary inspection by U.S. Customs and Border Protection officers after arriving at Logan Airport from the Dominican Republic on May 18. During a search of his cellphone, authorities allegedly found at least 20 photos and 952 videos depicting child sexual abuse materials.

The charge of transporting child pornography provides for a sentence of at least five years and up to 20 years in prison, at least five years and up to a lifetime of supervised release, and a fine of up to $250,000.

U.S. Attorney Leah B. Foley and Jeff Grimming, acting special agent in charge of Homeland Security Investigations in New England made the announcement Wednesday. Assistance was provided by U.S. Customs and Border Protection, Boston Field Office. Assistant U.S. Attorney Catherine Conroy of the Major Crimes Unit is prosecuting the case.

The details contained in the charging documents are allegations. The defendant is presumed to be innocent unless and until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in the court of law.

news_communities.title: Smiley has a surprising sprout in Lynn
news_communities.author: Olivia HaydarOlivia HaydarOlivia Haydar
news_communities.summary:
LYNN — Some plants are native to the Northeast; others, like the yucca, are not, yet one grown by a resident has thrived so much it looks almost like a Truffula tree out of “The Lorax.” 

A spiky green bush with leaves as sharp as knives, and a stalk rising from the middle of the plant with small white flower blossoms, takes center stage at the Smiley household. 

Ted Smiley has been tending his garden for more than two decades, but his garden doesn’t resemble the perennial landscapes common in the Northeast. Instead, it mimics the Southwest. 

Growing up on his grandparents’ flower farm, Smiley grew a deeper respect for plants that can withstand intense dry conditions and require little upkeep. The idea to recreate the Southwest on his front lawn, however, came when he moved to his home in Lynn. 

“When we got the house back in the ’90s, there was grass, but it was brown because it’s so hot and so dry, and it was impossible to keep the grass alive,” Smiley said. “So I thought, here’s my chance to grow some cactus and test. I was interested at the time in testing things and seeing what is not hardy up here so that I can push the limits and see what can grow.” 

Those limits have been pushed so far that the rare Yucca rostrata that he has been tending to for more than 20 years has skyrocketed over more than 15 feet tall with ethereal-looking white blossoms. 

“I look out the second-floor windows, and you see the flowers right there,” Smiley said. “It’s so weird.” 

Every morning, Smiley wakes up to a postcard-worthy garden full of cacti and succulents that are native to the Pacific Coast and Southwest. The yucca plant has taken center stage on Smiley’s front lawn, getting the most amount of possible sun rays, he said. 

“I placed it there with that in mind, because where it’s located it probably gets the most sun of anywhere on the property,” Smiley said. 

Smiley took it upon himself to dig up his entire front lawn and replace the soil with sand and rocks, re-creating the natural drainage system that allows the plant to thrive in the ground. 

“There’s no wet soil, full sun, a lot of heat, and the gravel that I used on the ground helps absorb the heat and creates this miniature desert, which is what I was aiming for,” Smiley said. 

The yucca genus is actually in the lily flower family, which results in them being extremely hardy in cold and heat resistance, according to Arthur Scarpa, the founder of the Cactus and Succulent Society of Massachusetts. 

In more than 60 years of growing cacti and succulents, and more specifically growing yuccas for 30 or so years, Scarpa has never seen a Yucca rostrata anywhere north of Philadelphia. 

Like Philadelphia, Lynn has a hardiness zone of seven, making it slightly warmer in the wintertime, Scarpa said, and for the rostrata species, they take decades to mature to the point of blooming as Smiley’s has. 

“It’s so slow growing that if you’re lucky, you buy one as a kid and it grows six feet by the time you’re retired… that’s doing pretty good,” Scarpa said. The difference in this situation is Scarpa has never seen a rostrata grow north directly in the ground. 

He believes that Smiley has struck gold with the plant and it’s deserving of a prize. 

“If it’s surviving in Lynn, he’s got a winner,” Scarpa said.

Scarpa said most species are native to areas like Mexico, but yuccas can thrive in the Northeast, such as the species Adam’s Needle (Yucca filamentosa). The rostrata species, however, is native to the mountainous cold areas in the southwest, like Colorado and New Mexico, he added. 

Scarpa believes that microclimates, which are areas where the temperature, wind, and humidity differ from the rest of the surrounding region, could explain why the yucca has grown so successfully. However, in an area in Lynn, close to the coast, it’s rare to see the Yucca rostrata species thrive in a humid and moist environment, even with the heat surge this summer. 

The best guess Scarpa has is the plant’s natural drainage system Smiley created with rocks and sand. 

“He’s obviously got the perfect situation there,” Scarpa said. 

Smiley said that his favorite part about having the yucca is not only the funky shape but how it contrasts with the surrounding cacti and succulents he’s planted around it. 

“I just like looking at it, and for a moment, if you look, it takes you to your favorite spot in the Southwest… It’s kind of like looking at a picture to me,” Smiley said.

news_communities.title: Lynnfield/Peabody youth take their star turns
news_communities.author: Deyscha SmithDeyscha SmithDeyscha Smith
news_communities.summary:
The Greater Boston Stage Company has announced their upcoming Young Company Summer Festival, which will feature 100 young performers, ranging from grade four through 12, in five fully staged musicals ranging from Disney classics to hits on Broadway.

This year, five youth from both Lynnfield and Peabody will participate in musical acts throughout August, including the production of “Footloose: The Musical” from Aug. 7-9, which will feature Lynnfield’s Belle M., who will play Rusty, as well as Peabody’s Allyson B., who has been casted as Eleanor Dunbar, and Peabody’s Stella L. as Ariel Moore.

“It’s really been so much fun, and it’s been great working on music and blocking and really learning strengthening our show,” Stella L. said. “Doing it with your friends is just such a great experience, too, because you know we’re just all having so much fun. It’s gonna be a great show.”

Directed by Tader Shipley, the musical is comprised of actors from grades 10-12, as well as the 2026 graduates, and is being choreographed by Erin Faria, music directed by Rena Marthaler, and stage managed by Madelyn Traynor.

On Aug. 14-16, two youth from Peabody have been casted in the family-friendly musical of “Disney’s The Little Mermaid JR,” including Emily K. as Carlotta and Emily W. as Andrina. The show, which will feature actors from grades four through six, will be directed by Katherine Gustafson, choreographed by Abigail Martin, music directed by Carrie Tully, and stage managed by Maisey O’Brien.

“Summer Festival is one of the highlights of our year,” said Autumn Blazon-Brown, director of education at Greater Boston Stage Company. “Over the course of just a few weeks, students build lasting friendships, develop confidence, strengthen their artistic skills, and create truly remarkable theatre together. Watching their growth from the first rehearsal to opening night is inspiring, and we can’t wait to share these productions with our community.”

The Greater Boston Stage Company is celebrating its 27th season of live theater, as well as the continuation of their classes, lessons, and fully staged productions through The Young Company at Greater Boston Stage Company, which is committed to helping the next generation of artists grow in their craft, serve as better audience members, help others, and even learn how to better collaborate and work together. Through the educational program, students will also further develop their skills as an actor, gain confidence, and establish a sense of self-discipline when working directly productions alongside professionals.

“You learn a lot about yourself as an actor and just a performer in general,” Stella L. said of her experience in the program thus far. “You learn what your strengths are and also the things you need to work on. It’s really great because you get to work with the creative teams and really strengthen what you want to work on this summer.”

This year’s Summer Festival provides students with a unique opportunity to learn and collaborate with professional directors, choreographers, designers, and theater artists, as well as receive intensive rehearsal and training. The event will also feature shows like “Singin’ in the Rain JR.,” and both “Disney’s Camp Rock The Musical,” and “The 25th Annual Putnam County Spelling Bee,” which tells the story of six middle school students who are competing for a spelling bee championship.

“We are incredibly proud of the hard work and artistry these students bring to the stage every summer,” Blazon-Brown said, adding: “The Summer Festival reflects everything the Young Company is about: artistic excellence, collaboration, creativity, and providing young people with professional-level opportunities in a supportive environment.”

news_communities.title: New cat shelter to open in Peabody this fall
news_communities.author: Amanda LureyAmanda LureyAmanda Lurey
news_communities.summary:
PEABODY — PALS Animal Life Savers and Salem Cat Aid are opening a cat shelter and rehabilitation center on Main Street in late September, creating a space dedicated to caring for North Shore cats that need extra time, medical care, or behavioral rehabilitation before they are ready for adoption. The center will also include a cat lounge and a cat food pantry.

Cass Warren — Salem Cat Aid founder, Co-founder of the new center, and a member of the PALS board of directors — explained that Salem Cat Aid began as an effort to feed stray cats in Salem before growing into a rescue organization that responds to injured, abandoned, and homeless cats. PALS shares that mission through a larger network of volunteers, foster homes, veterinary partnerships, and adoptions. The two organizations frequently work side by side to care for local animals.

The idea for a brick-and-mortar shelter became a necessity this spring.

PALS currently has 48 kittens and 26 adult cats, two of which are pregnant, leaving the organizations without enough foster space to keep pace with the growing need. So, when a suitable building became available in Peabody, Warren said the timing felt impossible to ignore.

Warren said the center is intended to serve cats that are often overlooked by traditional adoption programs.

“There are a lot of local shelters that won’t take cats that are above a certain age or have certain illnesses or especially have any behavioral issues,” Warren said. “A lot of local shelters will only take cats that are sweet, friendly lap cats, and so our rehabilitation is to turn the cats that have a little bit of spice to them into those sweeter, friendly cats.”

Beyond caring for cats awaiting adoption, the new space is intended to become a community gathering place. A large room inside the center will be transformed into a cat lounge where visitors can spend time with adoptable cats. Staff also hope to host kitten yoga, art nights, craft events, and educational programs.

The organizations are continuing renovations ahead of the planned September opening and are accepting donations and supplies through an Amazon wish list to help stock the center. They are also fundraising for monetary donations.

For Warren, whose full-time job is as a tattoo artist, cat rescue provides something entirely different.

“I connect really well with them. I understand their behavior really well, and so rescuing and fostering — it just, I don’t know — it does something for the soul that I can’t quite explain,” she said.

news_communities.title: Senate passes E-Bike Safety Policy
news_communities.author: Jim Mitchell
news_communities.summary:
Special to The Advocate

 

 

The state Senate this week passed an economic development package that regulates micromobility devices, including electric scooters and e-bikes by adopting an innovative speed-based framework to keep pace with rapidly evolving technology and address widespread safety concerns.

“E-bikes and other micromobility devices are an important part of our transportation system, giving an affordable way for residents to get to work, school, the grocery store, medical appointments, and connect with our public transportation system,” Senator Brendan Crighton (D-Lynn) said in a press release issued by his office.

“As Senate Chair of the Joint Committee on Transportation, I was proud to collaborate with stakeholders in municipal government, law enforcement, small business owners, and transportation advocates to build a framework that prioritizes safety for everyone on our roads, bike lanes, sidewalks, and trails,” Crighton said.

“Striking the right balance between accessibility and safety, this policy is a critical step to prevent serious Injuries and save lives.”

Recent advances in e-bike and electric scooter technology have rendered existing laws insufficient to ensure the safe use of these devices, according to Crighton.

This bill accounts for these developments by establishing universal and adaptable safety standards, along with further provisions that keep young children off of powered devices, some of which can reach speeds of 30 miles per hour, and ban mopeds and similar devices from operating in bike lanes and shared use paths.

The legislation establishes a multi-tiered speed-based system to apply standards and restrictions to each vehicle, ensuring that the bill includes more devices as they become available in the future.

Each speed tier has increased restrictions, ensuring that safety remains a top priority. The tiers apply standards of the types of safety features that must be built into the vehicle, safety requirements for vehicle operators, as well as right of way allowances.

Additionally, the bill includes a statewide 20 miles per hour default speed limit for shared use paths to reduce crashes, additional electrical safety standards on lithium-ion powered mopeds to prevent them from becoming fire hazards, and prohibition on operation of powered micromobility devices for children under 14 years of age to keep children off of the most dangerous devices.

It extends existing youth helmet law to all micromobility devices and requires all users regardless of age to wear protective headgear when operating anything above tier 0. The legislation also establishes a working group to iron out other priorities, such as updating the crash report form, and establishing a micro-ID pilot program.

The provisions in the economic development bill build off of the critical work and recommendations of the Special Commission on Micromobility which focused on providing much needed guidance for our cities and towns, promoting the responsible development of these new transportation options, and improving the safety of all road users.

Releasing their report in January 2026, the Commission reviewed current laws and regulations, making recommendations to support the expanding use of micromobility devices throughout the Commonwealth. Senator Crighton had the opportunity to serve as a commission member in his capacity as Senate Chair of the Joint Committee on Transportation. Other commission members included law enforcement, members of the Healey-Driscoll Administration, and transportation advocates.

The Senate passed the bill and sent it back to the House of Representatives for further consideration.

news_communities.title: Cracking down on collusion – Attorney General obtains $2.4 million settlement with school bus company that made false statements regarding school bus transportation contracts to several communities, including Saugus
news_communities.author: Jim Mitchell
news_communities.summary:
Massachusetts Attorney General Andrea Joy Campbell this week announced a $2.4 million settlement with student transportation services company Beacon Mobility Corporation, which operates through subsidiaries, including Van Pool Transportation LLC and NRT Bus, Inc., (collectively “Beacon”), to resolve allegations that the company colluded to allocate contracts — raising prices — and made false statements regarding school bus transportation contracts in the City of Lynn and Towns of Dedham and Saugus. In addition to the $2.4 million monetary payment, the majority of which will be distributed to the affected municipalities, the settlement requires Beacon to maintain an antitrust compliance program for at least five years and to notify the Attorney General’s Office (AGO) of any acquisitions of other transportation companies for 10 years. Beacon must also cooperate with the AGO in future investigations and must notify the AGO of any efforts by a competitor to enter into or enforce any agreement to allocate contracts, fix prices, rig bids or share competitively sensitive information related to student transportation contracts in Massachusetts.

“When companies engage in unlawful collusion that increase costs for municipalities, it reduces their ability to fund other critical programs including our libraries, public safety agencies and schools,” Campbell said in a press release issued by her office this week.

“My office is committed to investigating and eliminating illegal anticompetitive agreements that harm our communities,” she said.

The AGO was unable to provide information on the specific amount of money that Saugus would receive. Each municipality will receive compensation from the settlement that reflects the estimation of the damages incurred by the municipality as a result of the collusion.

Beacon is a student transportation services company registered in Delaware that provides special education transportation services to school districts in Massachusetts through its subsidiaries, including Van Pool Transportation LLC and NRT Bus, Inc.

The AGO alleges that in 2022 Beacon colluded with another student transportation services company in the region to raise prices on school districts by allocating contracts for the transportation of special education students in Saugus, Lynn and Dedham. Beacon did so by agreeing not to compete with the other company for contracts in certain towns in exchange for not facing competition from that company in other municipalities. The AGO also alleges that Beacon made false claims for payment by concealing its collusion and signing a certificate of non-collusion in Lynn.

“This vendor’s corrupt exploitation of our district’s efforts to get some of our most vulnerable students to school is shameful,” Lynn Mayor Jared C. Nicholson said. “We very much appreciate the Attorney General and her team for holding them accountable and returning their ill-gotten gains back to our taxpayers.”

Dedham Town Manager Leon I. Goodwin noted that his community has struggled with unsustainable cost increases for many goods and services, especially since the pandemic. “In order for us to provide safe and reliable services to our residents, we must have trust in our vendors and contractors, and this includes fair and transparent pricing because profits cannot come before people,” Goodwin said. “It is reassuring to see the Attorney General’s Office investigate one of the root causes of this issue and hold a company liable for their illegal actions.”

This case was handled by Assistant Attorney General Katherine Krems and Division Chief Anthony Mariano of the AGO’s Antitrust Division.

If you are aware of anticompetitive agreements to fix prices, allocate markets, rig bids or share competitively sensitive information in restraint of trade, please reach out to the AGO’s Antitrust Division at an*******@**ss.gov or by calling 617-727-8400.

news_communities.title: “An Isolated Occurrence”
news_communities.author: Jim Mitchell
news_communities.summary:
The Rt. 1 North restaurant that served nine drinks to the wrong-way driver before his fatal crash with state trooper defends its past record of no violations during ABCC hearing

 

By Mark E. Vogler

 

An attorney representing Tribu Mexican Kitchen & Bar on Rte. 1 North in Saugus – the bar that served free and afterhours drinks to an intoxicated customer on Cinco de Mayo before he killed himself and a state trooper in a wrong-way crash – asked the Alcoholic Beverages Control Commission (ABCC) to “keep the matter in context” before deciding disciplinary action against the restaurant. “This is an isolated occurrence,” Attorney Tracy Firicano told commissioners during a hearing this week (Tuesday, July 28) on Tribu’s multiple liquor law violations on the evening of May 5 and into the morning after.

“While there are numerous violations, context is important. The context of it being one evening,” she said.

Tribu served Hernan Ramon Marrero, 50, of Roslindale, nine alcoholic drinks during three-and-a-half hours shortly before the crash, according to ABCC investigators. At about 2:04 a.m., minutes after Marrero left the parking lot of the bar, he drove his Jeep Wrangler southbound on Route 1 North, colliding head-on with State Trooper Kevin Trainor. Both men died in the crash. Tests revealed that Marrero’s blood alcohol level was more than twice the legal limit.

“My clients are taking these violations very, very seriously,” Firicano told the commission.

“Sadly, two people lost their lives here. That’s a tragedy,” she said. “However, the issues before you, honorable commission members, are very narrow ones. And that doesn’t minimize the tragedy. All it does is keep it right-sized and narrows the focus on the evidence presented to you.”

After listening to the testimony at the hour-long hearing, commissioners said they would take the matter under advisement and issue a written opinion at a later date.

Once the ABCC completes its report, the Saugus Board of Selectmen – which acts as the town liquor licensing authority – will conduct its own hearing and will determine what disciplinary action should be taken against Tribu’s liquor license. The board could vote to suspend Tribu’s liquor license or even revoke it. Losing a liquor license for a substantial amount of time can financially hurt a restaurant’s business.

Most of this week’s hearing focused on a five-page report by Supervising Investigator Caroline L. Guarino, which she read into the record. The report, which was constructed by the use of surveillance video and information provided by Tribu, established a timeline from the moment that Marrero arrived at the bar at around 9:15 p.m. on May 5 and left the premises at 1:52 a.m. on May 6. The bar provided all credit card and cash payment records. From the video film and records, ABCC investigators were able to determine when Marrero was served his alcoholic drinks.

Marrero was only billed for two margaritas with Don Julio Reposado and food for a total of $71.69. He left a $30 tip for a total payment of $101.69, according to his credit card information.

The ABCC investigation determined that Marrero received five of his nine alcoholic drinks after midnight – the last one was served at 12:53 a.m. The investigation also concluded that Marrero only paid for two of his drinks. Serving free drinks and after hours are violations of state liquor law. Tribu committed 26 counts of serving alcoholic beverages after midnight and 31 counts of serving free drinks, according to the violations cited by the ABCC investigation.

In her report, Supervising Investigator Guarino noted that Marrero shared a special relationship with Herman Zambrano, one of the bartenders who was on duty on May 5-6. “I interviewed manager Zambrano in the presence of Attorney Firicano,” Guarino wrote.

“Zambrano stated that Marrero was his friend and mentor for over 20 years. Zambrano stated that he had been sober for 2 ½ years and on May 5, 2026, he started drinking alcoholic beverages,” she wrote.

Attorney Firicano elaborated on the friendship during the hearing. “He [Marrero] wasn’t your typical customer,” Firicano said.

The attorney called Marrero “a mentor” and “father-figure” to Zambrano. “They were very close,” she said.

The circumstances were different during that night of drinking at the bar, she stressed. “Mr. Zambrano never drank with employees, because he hadn’t drunk himself in up to two years,” she said. So, it was out of the ordinary for bar employees who were no longer working to receive free drinks, after hours with Zambrano.”

“These are in no ways to be excuses,” Firicano said.

She stressed that Tribu “has no prior violations of any kind” prior to the events of May 5-6. “You have no information that what happened was a regular occurrence,” said Firicano, who also noted that Tribu has cooperated with ABCC investigators and has already initiated steps “to ensure that no such violations occur in the future.

Tribu employs 23 people who are “hard-working” and who are “learning from this experience,” she said.

 

(Editor’s Note: This story was covered by a reporter who viewed the proceedings of the July 28 hearing broadcast on a computer site set up by the Massachusetts Alcoholic Beverages Control Commission. The ABCC arranged for the site, anticipating it would not be able to accommodate all interested parties in its hearing room at its Chelsea offices.)

news_communities.title: A Number One Team
news_communities.author: Jim Mitchell
news_communities.summary:
Saugus Sachems Track Camp finishes first among 18 teams competing in a Rhode Island track meet

 

By Mark E. Vogler

 

Six-year-old Charlie Tobies said she felt like she was part of something special this summer while learning how to hurdle, run and throw a javelin. “It was pretty good,” she said of her experience as a member of the Saugus Sachems Track Camp.

“All I know is that I made new friends. I liked that I got to do my events and hang out with other people I didn’t know,” said Charlie, who will be in the first grade when school resumes in the fall.

She will get to tell her new classmates what it was like to win a first-place medal in the javelin competition for kids her age or the second-place medal for the 400 meter run.

Charlie was one of 45 kids – many of them displaying athletic medals and ribbons – who celebrated as champions last week at William L. MacNeil Memorial Track and Field. Saugus Sachems Track Camp finished in first place among the 18 teams competing in the Sixth Annual CLCF Summer Showdown in Cranston, R.I., on July 18. This year’s finish was the best one for the group, which had previously finished third (2025), second (2024), third (2023) and third (2022) during its five years at the track meet.

“This group was unique in many ways,” said Coach Chris Tarantino, who has been organizing the track camp for 21 years. Despite a high turnover in participants, the camp had its biggest group of first-year participants, allowing a group of 64 young athletes to participate in the Cranston meet.

“This was also the widest range of ages as having more high school kids than we’ve had in the past,” Tarantino said. “But what really separated this group of kids was that resiliency dealing with unprecedented heat waves rescheduling torrential downpour nights and right before heading down to Rhode Island dealing with the impacts of the Canadian fires but through it all they came together bonded support each other worked exceptionally hard and earned the desired results.”

“Coach T.,” as he is affectionately known by people familiar with his track camp program, has a knack of involving parents, counselors and alumni as well as current Middle and High School track team members. Some of the older kids in the program assume coaching roles, passing on their knowledge to the younger athletes.

Elias Belkheira, 16, who will be going into his junior year at the Pioneer Charter School, competed in three different events this summer: the high jump, long jump and triple jump. “I compete, but my main focus was to counsel the kids,” Elias said.

“I mostly help out in the jumping. All of the kids interested in jumping come to me,” he said.

Nathalie Bonhomme has been watching her daughter, Aubrey Viciere, 14, participate in the track camp for five years. “I watched her enjoyment for the kids she coaches when they cross the finish line,” observed Bonhomme.

“She was more excited for them than herself. She took care of those kids like they were her own. She was a counselor to kids,” she said.

Tarantino praised Aubrey’s leadership skills in working with younger kids.

At last week’s get-together, several parents of first-time participants said they are impressed with how the track camp program helps their kids.

Rosetta DiPrizio credited the program with having a positive influence on her 12-year-old son, Dante. “I think it helped him grow self-esteem and confidence,” DiPrizio said.

“Coach T. and his coaches are phenomenal,” she said.

Nicole Connor, another parent of a first-year participant in the track camp, called it a great experience for her 12-year-old son Matthew. “I thought it was a great program and very well-organized,” Connor said.

“The coaches are very supportive and encouraging. And they’re good at meeting new parents,” she said.

Annalisa Ferrara, 12, has been competing at the track camp for six years. She won first again in the hurdles for her age category. “I like that I’m really good, and it’s also a lot of fun,” she said.

Her passion has affected her dad, Rob Ferrera, who has been coaching at the track camp for a couple of years. “When I was growing up, my father liked Little League coaching. He got me into it,” Ferrera said.

“I try to use his tools in talking to the kids and trying to get them to do things that they don’t think they can do. It’s a lot of fun and I forget about work when I come here,” he said.

Matthew Benoit, 12, and his three brothers – John, 13; James, 9 and Mark, 8 – participated again in this year’s track camp.

“I learned a lot and got better in all of my events,” Matthew said.

“And if anybody is interested in it, I would tell them it’s a lot of fun and you can do what you like to do. Even if you’re not fast, you can find an event that you can compete in,” he said.

Tarantino’s 14-year-old daughter, Naomi, said she has been involved in the track camp for 13 years. “I think it’s a great opportunity to try new things and have a great opportunity to compete,” she said.
