news_communities.title: Saugus Gardens in the Summer
news_communities.author: Jim Mitchell
news_communities.summary:
Here’s what’s blooming in town this week to make your walks more enjoyable

 

By Laura Eisener

 

Visitors to Saugus Iron Works in what is left of the summer will see some changes to the landscape but also some new activities that focus on nature in the park.

The upper lawn has an empty space this week due to the removal of the European beech tree (Fagus sylvatica). Often I have been told that this was the most-loved tree in the town, due to its location, size and dark wine-red foliage color. The tree predates the national park and was probably planted by a homeowner on Central Street in the late 19th century. People have tried to estimate the tree’s age by its size, or by memories of longtime residents. When the rings were counted, there were about 150, making it likely that the tree was planted in the late 1870s. The trunk was approximately six feet across at its base. The tree’s removal took several hours due to its size. Over the course of the day last Thursday, several Saugonians from the neighborhood, members of Saugus Garden Club, and others stopped by to pay their respects.

Sometimes called copper beech or purple beech, varieties of European beech with colorful foliage are among the most admired trees that can be grown in the Northeast. Most European beech trees have green leaves, but there are variations in leaf shape (cut-leaf varieties have almost feathery foliage, unlike the usual oval, slightly scalloped leaves); tree form (such as upright or weeping varieties); and color, including tricolor beech, which may have green, reddish, white and pink areas in the leaves. Beech were arguably the most desired trees in the last half of the 19th century, and old estates almost always had at least one beech planted near the front entrance. A few of these trees persist today in private gardens around town.

In recent decades, several diseases and environmental stresses have affected beech trees. The droughts of recent years add to diseases that affect our native American beech (Fagus grandifolia), the European beech planted in gardens, and the somewhat less often planted oriental beech (Fagus orientalis). Since the early 1900s, beech bark disease has become a problem in this area. This is a combination of an insect infestation of beech scale (Xylococcus betulae) and two species of Neonectria fungus species (Neonectria faginata and Neonectria ditissima). Much more recently, beech leaf disease has affected beech trees in forests and cultivated landscapes. Nematodes, which are tiny, often microscopic roundworms, are believed to be the cause of this. While most nematodes in our environment are benign and sometimes beneficial, the nematodes responsible for beech leaf disease (Litylenchus crenatae) cause harm by devouring and damaging leaf tissue as it emerges in spring. According to the Arnold Arboretum, there are a few bacteria and fungi connected with these nematodes that also play a part in the stress on beeches. Leaves often have discoloration between the veins, looking somewhat striped, and foliage can also look wrinkled or misshapen. It is easier to observe in green foliaged beech varieties than in those with darker leaves.

Other nearby institutions with valuable beech trees have also been struggling with these diseases, including Harvard’s Arnold Arboretum in Jamaica Plain, which has a sizeable beech tree collection. Current treatments include foliar spraying, trunk injection and root flare sprays of several fungicides. I first saw evidence of beech leaf disease at Glen Magna in Danvers, where the trees have been treated for several years and appear to be doing well. There are several American beech on that property and at least one weeping European beech that is a focal point of the grounds.

Despite treatments, the tree at the Iron Works had lost some of its lower foliage due to the beech leaf disease in recent years. On July 4 I was sitting under the tree, relaxing in the shade after enjoying the 250th celebration, when one of the dead branches fell on me. Other dead branches were immediately pruned by park staff, and evaluation of the tree health intensified, leading to the sad decision to remove the tree. Several people came to say goodbye before or while the tree was being removed by Iron Tree Service of Beverly, including several members of the Saugus Garden Club.

Anyone with beech trees on their property would want to have their trees examined because many of the local beeches have one or more health problems and could be at risk. Early intervention may be able to prolong the lives of some trees.

On a happier note, two of the new staff members at Saugus Iron Works have begun developing children’s “pop up” programs about nature at the Iron Works. Saugus Iron Works intern/Essex Heritage River steward Valentina Sierra and national park ranger Gracie Wood had a display about pollinators last week, which included pictures and facts about some local pollinating insects and hummingbirds and the plants they pollinate, as well as opportunities for children to draw on paper some of the plants and pollinators they learned about. Earlier, the two held a pop-up that focused on fish in the Saugus River and gave the kids a chance to make fish prints. Future programs this summer, mostly held on Thursday mornings, will likely focus on butterfly-friendly plants, colonial New England games, early American gardens, and as fall approaches changing autumn leaves. Families are invited to stop by after the library’s children’s events at the Iron Works and check out these special programs.

news_communities.title: The Sounds of Saugus
news_communities.author: Jim Mitchell
news_communities.summary:
By Mark E. Vogler

 

Good morning, Saugus

Practically any area resident who watches a Boston television station or listens to the local news on the radio or reads The Saugus Advocate regularly, knows by now that a Saugus restaurant on Route 1 North served nine alcoholic drinks in the final hours of Cinco de Mayo (May 5) to a customer who went out and killed himself and state Trooper Kevin T. Trainor in a head-on wrong-way collision on Route 1 North in Lynnfield. People who are following the story also know that 50-year-old Hernan Ramon Marrero of Roslindale was highly intoxicated when he drove away from the parking lot of Tribu Mexican Kitchen & Bar in his 2018 Jeep Wrangler early May 6. Tests show that his blood alcohol level was more than twice the legal limit. That Marrero was legally drunk and shouldn’t have been driving are indisputable facts.

It’s also clear that this tragic incident has captivated the public outrage over the senseless death of a 30-year-old state trooper who was engaged to be married, who happened to be on his way home after responding to the report of a wrong-way driver. On Wednesday morning, shortly before press time, 150 people had let their emotions be known on The Advocate Newspapers Facebook Site. Close to 100 of our readers weighed in with comments to accompany their emojis, many of them calling for the restaurant – especially the bartender staff that served the drinks – to be held accountable for the crash that killed the young state trooper.

I drive up and down Route 1 several times a week. And I know that I will always be thinking about this tragedy anytime I drive past the restaurant at 44 Broadway (Route 1 North). It will be hard not to think about the death of a state trooper responding to a wrong-way crash a short distance up the road in Lynnfield.

It was surely a fatal crash that could have been avoided had Marrero gotten a cab that night instead of driving away. Or, if the bar stopped serving him when it was obvious he had way too much to drink and was in no shape to drive home. Somebody who was around Marrero that night should have stopped him from driving away. A cab ride to a local motel would have been the right thing to do. It’s easy to look back now and say what “could have” or “should have” been done.

Tribu, the restaurant where Marrero spent the final hours of his life, has already paid dearly for the tragedy through adverse publicity. Meanwhile, it also risks having its license suspended or worse.

Hopefully, this tragedy is never forgotten and serves as a sobering reminder to the masses about the potential consequences of drunk driving and the responsibility that all of us share in making sure that family, relatives, friends and other people don’t get behind the wheel of a car when it’s obvious that they had too much to drink.

Stay tuned.

 

Election alert: Sept. 1 primary coming

Town Clerk Ellen Schena and her staff have about four weeks to complete preparation for the upcoming Sept. 1 primary election. A major order of business is signing up enough election workers – both paid and volunteers.

Every two years, there is a state election that involves a September primary. With school not being in session yet, it becomes more challenging for the Town Clerk to recruit civic-minded Saugus High School juniors and seniors. So a flyer began circulating headlined “CALLING ALL SAUGUS HIGH JUNIORS AND SENIORS,” with the hopes of attracting civic-minded teens who want to help the elections run smoothly this fall: the State Primary (Sept. 1) and the Nov. 3 State General Election.

“Come work for Community Services to fulfill your high school hours OR you can be a Paid $$$$$$ Election Worker,” the flyer stated.

For those Saugus juniors and seniors who are interested in being paid or volunteer election workers, here are the particulars:

  • 16 years old can work part-time shifts (6 to 8 hours)
  • 17 & 18 year olds can work full shifts (8 to 12 hours)
  • The Town Clerk’s Office can accommodate any hours for interested students.

“Great to have on your College Applications/Resumes,” the flyer noted.

Those who are interested should stop by Town Hall or contact the Town Clerk’s Office to apply to work. Ask for Jacey Ruisi, Saugus Election Coordinator, at 781-231-4102 for more details.

A second flyer went out directed at adults who want to work the polls and earn some extra cash. The Town Clerk’s Office is looking to fill specific shifts: all day, or 6 a.m. to 2 p.m., 2 p.m. to 9 p.m. or swing shifts (accommodating hours). For those who are interested in applying for any of those paid positions, please contact the Town Clerk’s Office at 781-231-4102 or 4013.

 

Saugus United Parish Food Pantry

The Saugus United Parish Food Pantry will be open today (Friday, July 31), from 9:30-11 a.m. at 50 Essex St. in the basement of Cliftondale Congregational Church. The food pantry welcomes all neighbors facing food insecurity on Friday mornings. Volunteers are also welcome. Please call the Food Pantry Office (781-233-2663) or go to the website (cliftondalecc.org) for details.

 

Cars and Cops Show tomorrow

The Seventh Annual Cars and Cops Car Show is set for tomorrow (Saturday, Aug. 1), from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. in the parking lot of the Saugus Middle-High School at 1 Pierce Memorial Drive. The rain date is Aug. 8. The Cars and Cops Car Show of Massachusetts is a widely known family fun car show that occurs every year in the summer, put on by Saugus Police Officer Domenic Montano and his amazing team that wants to give back to their community.

The Cars and Cops Car Show of Massachusetts first started in September of 2018 and grew yearly. What originally started as a 100-125 vehicle car show grew to 300-plus cars in 2021.

 

This week’s “Shout Outs”

We received no nominations from readers this week. So I will exercise my editorial prerogative to highlight the collective efforts of adult and youth volunteers involved in the various youth activities that are happening around town, especially athletic events. Countless adult volunteers are making contributions to the betterment of Saugus every day during the summer months. Hats off to those people.

 

Want to “Shout Out” a fellow Saugonian?

This is an opportunity for our paper’s readers to single out – in a brief mention – remarkable acts or achievements by Saugus residents or an act of kindness or a nice gesture. Just send an email (mv***@*****st.net) with a mention in the subject line of “An Extra Shout Out.” No more than a paragraph; anything longer might lend itself to a story and/or a photo.

 

Free Summer concerts series continues

You know it’s truly summer in Saugus when the Wednesday night crowds start to gather at the Saugus Iron Works National Historic Site, where they sing, clap and dance to the music. It’s that time of year again. Another summer of free outdoor concerts over an eight-week period at the Iron Works began on July 1.

This marks the fifth consecutive summer that the Saugus Public Library and the National Park Service are collaborating on a local outdoor event that seems to get more popular every year. The Saugus Cultural Council (a local arm of the Mass Cultural Council, a state agency) is also a key sponsor of the event. The concerts are free and open to the public. The concert series celebrates local musical talents in Essex County and creates opportunities for residents and visitors to engage with the park during evening hours.

Shows begin at 6 p.m. each Wednesday in August. People can bring blankets and chairs, snacks, etc. Don’t forget to bring a friend, too, to enjoy a couple of hours of music outdoors. The events take place on the stage behind the museum building, and spectators can settle down on the upper lawn. It is suitable for all ages. Restrooms are available until nearly 8 p.m. when the concerts conclude. If weather looks bad for any particular Wednesday, concertgoers are urged to check the library website (www.sauguspubliclibrary.org), which will update for cancellations on that day.

This year’s lineup features a combination of new bands and familiar faces. Concerts begin at 6 p.m. on the Big Lawn each Wednesday through August 19. This week’s scheduled headliner (July 29) was Ditto Band, which specializes in Acoustic American Rock. Here is the rest of the schedule for the summer concert series:

  • August 5: The Implications (Rock & Country).
  • August 12: Squeezebox Stompers (Cajun, Zydeco, Blues, Folk).
  • August 19: Coco Brown & The Invitation (Motown & Soul).

Watch https://sauguspubliclibrary.org for weather updates and cancellations.

 

Starlight Cinema Tuesday night

Saugus Community Television invites residents of all ages to enjoy an evening of family fun under the stars at its annual Starlight Cinema Movie Night next Tuesday, Aug. 4. The original show date (July 28) was cancelled this week. This year’s featured film is the beloved family adventure “Jumanji” (1995), starring Robin Williams. The movie is about a magical board game that brings jungle dangers to life. The event will be held at Parcher Field, located next to the Kasabuski Rink behind Target. Family activities begin at 5:30 p.m., and the movie will start promptly at 7:30 p.m.

This year’s event will feature a large LED movie screen, allowing the film to begin before sunset while still providing an outstanding viewing experience for everyone in attendance. The earlier starting time makes it easier for families with young children to enjoy the evening and return home at a reasonable hour.

Starlight Cinema is a free community event open to everyone. Complimentary popcorn will be provided, while supplies last, and guests are welcome to bring their own snacks and nonalcoholic beverages. A variety of food and dessert options from local food vendors will be available for purchase throughout the evening. Featured vendors: Tiffany’s Tasty Treats, offering gourmet brownies, cookies and gluten-free and sugar-free desserts; Bono Appetit, serving specialty sandwiches, including pulled pork grilled cheese and paninis; and Soc’s Ice Cream, featuring refreshing frozen treats for a summer evening.

Beginning at 5:30 p.m., families can enjoy a variety of free activities: interactive games displayed on the LED screen, a festive photo booth featuring a giant popcorn-themed arch, giant Jenga and other family-friendly entertainment. Local businesses and community organizations will also be on hand with informational displays, giveaways and activities.

Saugus Television will offer exclusive Starlight Cinema commemorative T-shirts for purchase. The shirts feature an original design created exclusively for the event by Saugus Television’s own John Prudent. Attendees will be able to select their preferred shirt size, and the shirts will be custom printed. Shirts will also be available during Saugus Founders Day for those who are unable to attend the movie night.

Starlight Cinema is made possible through the generous support of the Saugus Cultural Council, Richard A. Kowalsky Insurance Agency, Inc., community partners, local businesses and sponsors. Saugus Television is currently seeking additional sponsors to help support this free community event. Businesses and organizations interested in sponsorship opportunities are encouraged to contact Saugus Television for more information.

Volunteers are also needed to assist with event setup, activities and operations throughout the evening. Anyone interested in volunteering is encouraged to contact Maureen Whitcomb at Saugus Community Television.

Building on the anticipated success of this year’s event, Saugus Television hopes to continue the Starlight Cinema series with a special Halloween-themed movie night later this year.

“This is the first time Saugus is doing the movie,” said Whitcomb, the station’s administrative assistant.

“Saugus TV wants to do a second one for Halloween, then wants to continue them next summer too. Similar to Wakefield and surrounding towns,” she said.

Additional details will be announced as plans are finalized. Continued community support through sponsorships and volunteers will help make future free family events possible.

Residents are encouraged to bring lawn chairs, blankets and bug spray and to gather with family and friends for an evening of outdoor entertainment, community spirit and summertime fun.

For more information about Starlight Cinema, sponsorship opportunities or volunteer opportunities, please contact Saugus Community Television.

 

KOC Crafts fair Aug. 8

The Saugus Knights of Columbus No. 1829 will host a crafts fair on Saturday, Aug. 8, from 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. at 57 Appleton St. in Saugus: baked goods, candles, handmade textiles, jewelry, wood carving and much more. Visitors can also enjoy making their own sundaes or enjoy popcorn, hot dogs, hot coffee, donuts and raffles.

 

Summer Reading time at the library

The 2026 Summer Reading Program at the Saugus Public Library is underway and will last through Friday, Aug. 21. Here’s a summary of the program:

WHO: Kids Pre-K through 6th grade.

WHAT: Kids read the books they love, log their reading and earn prizes! They’ll enjoy reading what they love, free programs, crafts and activities.

WHY: Don’t lose those hard-earned skills! Summer reading plays a vital role in helping reduce the “Summer Slide” – the learning loss experienced between school years – which can leave students significantly behind their peers. The Saugus Public Schools recommend kids read at least 20 minutes every day. We also recommend reading to your child, even as they become an independent reader. Talk about what you’ve read together. Help them find books they like – we can help with that. Make it a fun part of a daily routine they look forward to!

PRIZES: Every reader wins prizes, and books to keep. We’ll also raffle vouchers for ice cream, pizza, roller skating, mini golf, bowling and much more. Grand prize drawings include tickets to Canobie Lake Park and Nova Adventure Park!

HOW: Download the Beanstack App!

  • CREATE AN ACCOUNT: If this is your first time participating in one of the SPL’s reading challenges using Beanstack, here are step-by-step instructions [https://www.loom.com/share/0efe0cc7c0f64b96b3c0a38ade8b04f6] on how to create a Beanstack account. If you’ve used Beanstack before, simply register for our 2026 Summer Reading Challenge.
  • REGISTER FOR A CHALLENGE: This video [https://www.loom.com/share/9cfd52f03a4c4444bc9ab86d94b51cea] will show you how to register for a reading challenge using the app.
  • LOG YOUR READING: This video [https://www.loom.com/share/fda67bebf80e443faaad2529fa3ca486] will show you how to log your reading using the mobile app.
  • FROM A COMPUTER: If you prefer not to use the app, here’s a link to access the SPL’s 2026 Kids Summer Reading Challenge using a computer. Beanstack Link [https://sauguspubliclibrary.beanstack.com/reader365]
  • Or Register in Person: Stop by the library to register in person and use our paper reading log.
  • Download free e-books and e-audiobooks from the library!

Can’t make it to the library? Our digital collections provide easy access to the books kids love, 24 hours a day seven days a week. Download free, fresh titles all summer using the hoopla and Libby apps! [https://www.sauguspubliclibrary.org/children/family]

 

Veterans Day Bricks Program is Back

The Saugus Veterans Council is pleased to reinstate the Brick Program! After our vendor retired last year (thank you, Del from Pavlok, for working with us over the years), we have found another engraver who will be taking our orders for Veterans Day! Proceeds from the brick sales are devoted to the upkeep of Saugus Veterans Park. If you are interested in purchasing a brick, a 4×8″ is $100 (three lines) and an 8×8″ (five lines) is $200. Please contact Corinne Riley (781-231-7995) for an application or more information. All orders must be in no later than Sept. 10.

news_communities.title: Legislature Creates New License Plate for Families of Fallen Law Enforcement Officers
news_communities.author: Jim Mitchell
news_communities.summary:
Special recognition would help immediate family honor their loved ones

 

BOSTON — The Massachusetts Legislature yesterday passed legislation to create a new special license plate to honor the memories of fallen law enforcement officers by offering a symbol of respect to their surviving spouses, parents, and children.

 

The bill—S.2903, An Act honoring Blue Star Families—directs the Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) to create a new Blue Star Families plate to help the family members remember their loved one in a visible way on their car. It would also create a Blue Star Family emblem for motorcycle plates.

 

“Every day, law enforcement officers across the Commonwealth put themselves between danger and the people they serve. These heroes left their families in the morning and never came home,” said Senate President Karen E. Spilka (D-Ashland). “This bill won’t erase these tragic and heartbreaking losses, but it will ensure their memory, and the memories of all our fallen officers, travel with the families who carry it every day. I’m grateful to Chair Rodrigues, Chair Crighton, and Senator Mark for their advocacy on this legislation, and to our colleagues in the House of Representatives for getting this to the Governor’s desk.”

 

“This bill is about recognizing the sacrifice made by the families of fallen law enforcement officers,” said House Speaker Ronald J. Mariano (D-Quincy). “By making license plates available to the spouses, parents, and children of law enforcement who were killed in the line of duty, Massachusetts is ensuring that the legacy of those who gave their lives in service to our communities is never forgotten. I would like to thank Chairman Arciero, Chairman Walsh, and our partners in the Senate for their work in getting this important bill to the Governor’s desk for her signature.”

 

“Growing up in a law enforcement family, I know that when an officer puts on the uniform, their entire family shares in that commitment to public service. We can never fully repay the families who have lost a loved one in the line of duty, but we can ensure their sacrifice is always remembered. This Blue Star Family license plate is a lasting tribute to the heroes we have lost and a visible reminder that the Commonwealth stands with the spouses, parents, and children who carry their loved one’s legacy forward every day. Their sacrifice will never be forgotten,” said Representative Jessica Ann Giannino (D-Revere).

 

“I am honored to have worked with my colleagues to enact a specialty license plate available to the families of fallen police officers. This seemingly small gesture is an important recognition of the amazing sacrifice made by the fallen and their families. As the bible says, ‘Greater love than this hath no man than he lay down his life for a friend,’” said Representative Jeffrey Rosario Turco (D-Winthrop).

 

“Honoring the law enforcement officers we have lost in the line of duty with the Blue Star Families plate is a meaningful way for their loved ones to carry on their memory,” said Senator Brendan Crighton (D-Lynn), Senate Chair of the Joint Committee on Transportation. “I was proud to join my colleagues in voting for this legislation, and I am thankful to the entire law enforcement community, especially our Blue Star Families, for their sacrifices.”

 

“Blue Star Families have endured the unimaginable loss of a child, spouse, parent, or sibling in the line of duty,” said Representative James Arciero (D-Westford), House Chair of the Joint Committee on Transportation. “While no symbol can fully express the gratitude owed to our fallen heroes and their loved ones, this legislation stands as a lasting commitment that their sacrifice and service will never be forgotten. Thank you to House Speaker Mariano, Chairman Michlewitz and Representative Walsh for their leadership on this bill to honor the Commonwealth’s Blue Star Families.”

 

Under the legislation, the RMV would be required to make the plates available to Blue Star spouses, parents, and children without charge. The RMV would also be able to offer vanity plate registrations for Blue Star plates up to six characters in length.

 

The Blue Star Family license plates would join other special recognition plates currently offered by the RMV, including Gold Star Family plates for drivers with close family members who died as a result of their service in the armed forces.

 

Having passed the Legislature, the bill was sent to Governor Maura Healey and was signed into law on 7/15/2026.

news_communities.title: Massachusetts House Passes Animal Welfare Bill
news_communities.author: Jim Mitchell
news_communities.summary:
Bill strengthens animal welfare protections, modernizes veterinary technician licensing, and supports responsible pet ownership

 

BOSTON – The Massachusetts House of Representatives today passed legislation to strengthen animal welfare, modernize veterinary care, improve consumer protections, and support responsible pet ownership across the Commonwealth.

 

“This legislation modernizes the Commonwealth’s animal welfare laws while supporting responsible pet ownership, strengthening veterinary care, protecting consumers, and while ensuring stronger enforcement of existing animal protection laws,” said House Speaker Ronald J. Mariano (D-Quincy). “I want to thank Chairman Lewis and the many bill sponsors for their work on this legislation, as well as all my colleagues in the House for recognizing the need for these important reforms.”

 

“If there is any issue that we can all agree on, it’s that all of our furry friends deserve long, happy lives,” said Representative Jack Patrick Lewis (D-Framingham), House Chair of the Joint Committee on Municipalities and Regional Government. “This legislation is a strong step towards that goal. We are employing robust measures to promote good caretaking and penalize bad actors, such as expanding policy related to veterinary technicians and pet insurance, banning the use of animals in household product safety research, and adding new oversight to the kennel industry. I am especially proud of the wide bipartisan support that this bill garnered, highlighting our collective unity on this issue. Thank you to Speaker Mariano, Chairman Michlewitz, and the many legislators that contributed to this outstanding legislation.”

 

“Animals enrich our lives in countless ways, and they deserve to be treated with compassion, dignity, and care. This legislation strengthens protections against abuse and neglect, modernizes veterinary care, supports responsible pet ownership, and ensures our laws reflect both the needs of today’s families and the welfare of the animals they love. I’m proud to support this important bipartisan effort to make Massachusetts a leader in animal welfare,” said Representative Jessica Giannino (D-Revere).

 

“As a life-long pet owner, I am happy to have supported this legislation which modernizes the Commonwealth’s laws for animal ownership, treatment and care. This bill is a comprehensive update to our law which will benefit our furry friends,” said Representative Jeffrey Rosario Turco (D-Winthrop).

 

The bill also modernizes the Commonwealth’s dog licensing and kennel oversight laws by strengthening inspection requirements, by improving reporting from licensing authorities, and by ensuring that dogs housed in kennels are properly licensed. The legislation provides practical updates for licensed kennels by allowing alternative forms of identification, such as microchips, under specified circumstances, while maintaining accountability and traceability for animals in their care.

 

To strengthen animal protection, the legislation establishes a clearer legal process for addressing cases of animal neglect. Law enforcement and animal control officers will be able to petition courts for timely intervention when animals are suffering from neglect, allowing courts to order appropriate care, remove animals from dangerous situations when necessary, or permanently prohibit individuals from owning animals in serious cases.

 

The bill strengthens protections for animals used in research by expanding adoption opportunities for dogs and cats after research concludes, and by increasing public reporting. The bill prohibits a manufacturer or contract testing facility from using a traditional animal test method if there is an alternative test method when testing a product, product formulation, chemical or ingredient. The bill also updates Massachusetts law governing pet insurance by adopting nationally recognized consumer protection standards.

 

The legislation establishes a statewide pet ownership program for older adults living in public housing. The program prohibits blanket bans on pets while allowing housing authorities to adopt reasonable pet policies that protect residents, animals, and housing facilities. An advisory group will develop recommendations to support the implementation of the program.

 

The bill further improves accessibility for individuals with disabilities by establishing meaningful penalties for transportation network companies (TNC) and drivers who unlawfully refuse service to riders accompanied by service animals, and ensuring stronger enforcement of existing accessibility requirements.

 

The bill creates a statewide licensing framework for veterinary technicians under the Board of Registration in Veterinary Medicine. The legislation expands the Board to include licensed veterinary technicians, establishes professional licensing standards, creates temporary licensure pathways, and provides a transition period to ensure the profession is fully licensed by 2031.

 

The legislation makes significant investments in animal health and welfare by expanding the allowable uses of the Homeless Animal Prevention and Care Fund, and by directing additional revenue from animal health and livestock disease enforcement fines into the fund to support programs that improve animal care throughout Massachusetts.

 

The bill passed the House of Representatives 151-1 and now goes back to the Senate for further consideration.

news_communities.title: Environmental Remediation Underway at Former Everett High School
news_communities.author: Independent Staff
news_communities.summary:
Special to the Independent

Environmental remediation is underway at the former Everett High School at 548 Broadway as the City takes an important step toward preparing the building for future use.

While the former Everett High School closed in 2007, portions of the building have remained in regular use over the years. Other areas, however, have sat vacant for nearly two decades. Walking through those sections today reveals just how much time has passed. Floors have buckled, debris from deteriorating ceilings has collected in classrooms, and computers from the early 2000s still sit where they were left. Some rooms feel as though they were frozen in time, while others show the visible effects of years without regular use. In one science lab, broken glass covers part of the floor while lab tables, equipment, and classroom materials remain intact on the other side. The conditions highlight why environmental remediation is necessary before these spaces can safely be brought back into service.

The project is being funded through a one-time grant, allowing the City to complete the work without impacting the local operating budget. The remediation will help bring previously unused portions of the building up to today’s standards and preserve the property for future use.

“When I walked through one of the classrooms, my first thought was, ‘It’s sad we let it get this far,’” said Mayor Robert J. Van Campen. “This building has been part of Everett’s history for generations, and we have a responsibility to take care of it. Whether it ultimately becomes part of our long-term solution to school overcrowding or serves another community purpose, preparing it now gives us options for the future.”

As the City works to address school overcrowding, one option under consideration is converting the former Everett High School into a middle school. The City is also evaluating the former Pope John XXIII High School property before any final decisions are made.

The City wants to reassure residents that the areas occupied by students and staff over the years have remained safe for use. The work taking place today is focused on preparing previously unused sections of the building for future occupancy.

To accommodate the project, the Wellness Center at the former Everett High School closed in June when remediation work began. The Eliot Family Resource Center has also been temporarily relocated during construction. Work on the building’s first floor and lower level is expected to be completed by September, with the Wellness Center anticipated to reopen around that time. The full remediation project is expected to continue through October as part of a multi-phase effort.

By completing this work now, the City is preserving an important community asset while ensuring it has more options to meet Everett’s future needs. No final decision has been made about the building’s long-term use, but the remediation will ensure it is ready for whatever comes next.

news_communities.title: DiDomenico Secures $5 million and Key Legislative Wins in Senate Economic Development Bill
news_communities.author: Independent Staff
news_communities.summary:
Special to the Independent

Senator Sal DiDomenico secured language in the Senate Economic Development bill for several of his key policy priorities, and he brought $5 million in bond authorizations for local infrastructure projects in the district. The economic development package lifts up small businesses and burgeoning industries, bans predatory kiosks used in cryptocurrency scams, and reins in the potential dangers of artificial intelligence by instituting responsible guardrails against catastrophes.

DiDomenico secured several of his own proposed bills in the Economic Development bill

• ENOUGH Act bill that will create an innovative strategy to fight poverty by investing resources in high need neighborhoods and collaborating with community residents to help drive decisions that will ensure investments increase economic mobility.

• E-Bike classification bill that will classify and expand access to more electric bikes across Massachusetts.

• Physical Therapy Licensure Compact bill that will allow physical therapists from other states participating in the compact to practice in Massachusetts without having to endure the relicensing process, and for our physical therapists to do the same in those states.

DiDomenico secured $5 million in bond authorizations for these local infrastructure projects

• $2.5 million to the city of Chelsea for design and construction of a culvert.

• $2.5 million to the city of Everett for subsurface infrastructure improvements.

“I am thrilled to pass three important pieces of legislation I filed so that we can address poverty head on, support health care workers, and empower more people to bike safely across our state,” said Senator Sal N. DiDomenico. “The bond funding I got authorized for local projects has the potential to support my district’s cities in critical infrastructure improvement plans that will benefit residents in our communities and beyond. This package will do so much for our economy, small businesses, and residents across my district, and I look forward to fighting for all this language in the conference committee.”

The bill also surges the production of new housing units through automatic two-family zoning across Massachusetts, creates safety rules for fast electric scooters and e-bikes, and invests $100 million in immediate support for scientific research programs at public higher education institutions.

With $575.4 million in authorizations, the economic development bond bill is poised to grow quality jobs in the Commonwealth, support innovation, and improve the quality of life for workers and families.

The bill prioritizes bonding investments to boost every aspect of the Massachusetts economy, including:

 • $100 million to support and promote economic growth and job creation in the defense sector;

• $75 million to support the development and application of AI;

• $25 million to support downtown and main street vitality in Massachusetts towns and cities, in addition to $2.5 million to help convert vacant storefronts into pop-up opportunities for new small businesses;

• $25 million for research and development of robotics technology;

• $20 million to support construction of early stage and high growth business ventures;

• $20 million to support community development financial institutions and small businesses; and

• $25 million to support arts, culture, and the creative economy, building on recent successes of the Massachusetts tourism and cultural sector.

The legislation requires major AI developers—known as large frontier developers—to account for their AI models’ risk of critical safety incidents by setting frameworks to avoid potential catastrophes. The Attorney General’s Office (AGO) would be empowered to bring civil lawsuits against major AI developers if they violate these new safety requirements.

The bill would create unprecedented levels of new housing units in Massachusetts by allowing two-family homes on all residentially zoned lots, subject to reasonable local limitations.

Supporting the Massachusetts economy’s workers and their families, the bill goes further to boost the state’s housing stock by creating a new, easier process for converting commercial properties into residential units, and requiring timely review processes for housing construction projects.

Recent e-bike and electric scooter technology has moved beyond older state laws into unregulated territory. This bill accounts for these developments by creating new safety standards that keep young children off these devices, some of which can speed at 30 miles per hour, and banning mopeds and similar devices from bike lanes and shared use paths. 

Scientific research drives a significant part of the Massachusetts economy. With federal research funding under threat, the legislation invests an immediate $100 million in bridge funding for public higher education institutions to help maintain the pace of scientific discovery and retain talented graduate and post doctorate workers.

Over the course of two days of debate, the Senate built on the underlying bill by adopting amendments in critical areas related to responsible technological advancement, the hospitality industry and vibrant business districts, and the ability for certain professions to work across state lines.

Safety in Technological

Innovation

Stopping Cryptocurrency ATM Misuse (Amendment 374): Responds to the use of cryptocurrency kiosks as tools in predatory scams by fully banning the operation of such kiosks in Massachusetts. Scammers in recent years have directed older adults to use crypto kiosks to send money which is often not recoverable when the fraud is discovered, leading some seniors to lose their entire life savings.

Frontier AI Risk Reports and Independent Verification (Amendment 471): Verifies that large AI developers are complying with this legislation’s new safety requirements by requiring independent, third-party safety audits. Additionally requires large AI companies to undergo in-depth, independent safety testing every four months to identify any residual catastrophic risks.

Protecting Against CSAM (Amendment 94): Criminalizes the creation, possession, or sharing of AI-generated child sexual abuse material (CSAM), in response to new AI technology and computer programs capable of generating synthetic images that are indistinguishable from real photos. Penalties for sharing such images go up to 10 years imprisonment. Creating or prompting synthetic CSAM is punishable by up to five years in prison, or 10 years if the image depicts a real child.

Responsible Robotics (Amendment 118): Ensures the responsible use of robotics technology. Prohibits the possession, operation, manufacture, or sale of robots that are equipped with weapons—including firearms, chemical agents, weaponized lasers and explosives. Prohibits the use of a robotic device to criminally harass or physically restrain another person. Violations are punishable by up to five years in prison. Includes a waiver process for defense companies and contractors; an exemption for the military; and a process for law enforcement to use weaponized robots to destroy or diffuse bombs, with a proper warrant.

The ‘Fun Agenda’

No Soccer No Party (Amendment 595): Convenes a working group to study the feasibility of a future international soccer tournament to be held in Massachusetts. The group, organized under the Office of International Trade and Investment, would study potential dates, venues, operational needs, and funding sources, and would coordinate with representatives of participating countries including the United States, Scotland, and nations with a significant diaspora in Massachusetts.

Making music affordable by reining in predatory ticket scalping (Amendment 20): Institutes a 110 per cent cap on prices charged by ticket resale platforms for music concert tickets.

Happy Hour (Amendment 78): Gives cities and towns the option of re-establishing ‘happy hour’ discounted alcohol sales policies, boosting bars, restaurants, and other licensed establishments. Municipalities would regulate happy hours by local ordinance.

Conviviality Districts (Amendment 309): Builds on the success of a historic summer by permanently allowing cities and towns to permit public alcohol consumption in designated outdoor districts. Municipalities would be able to adopt the local-option districts for areas such as streets and parks, with the requirement that drinks be purchased from licensed establishments within the designated area.

Public Arts and Entertainment Microgrant Program (Amendment 354): Authorizes $1 million for a new grant program to boost the cultural and economic vitality of downtown areas, commercial areas, cultural districts, gathering places, and nightlife destinations. The Massachusetts Cultural Council would distribute the microgrants to support public arts, performances, and programming.

Cultivating Agritourism Across Massachusetts (Amendment 70): Authorizes $5 million for grants to support local farms, agriculture, and small businesses through agritourism.

Massport Liquor License Flexibility (Amendment 441): Allows bars and restaurants at Logan Airport to continue serving alcohol as long as flights are arriving and departing from the airport.

Networking Jobs Across State Lines

Psychology Interjurisdictional Compact (Amendment 11): Increases access to psychology services by adding Massachusetts to an interstate compact that recognizes the licensure of psychologists in other participating states. Allows licensed psychologists from those states to practice via telehealth across state lines.

Social Work Licensure Compact (Amendment 222): Supports Massachusetts social workers by joining surrounding states in the social work licensure compact, ensuring they can continue to care for patients in other states.

Establishing a Physical Therapy Compact (Amendment 402): Bolsters the physical therapy workforce by working toward the creation of an interstate compact, which would allow licensed physical therapists and assistants to practice across participating state lines. 

Fostering a Strong Local

and Regional Economy

Juvenile Jurisdiction (Amendment 495): Raises the age of juvenile jurisdiction to include residents who are 18 years old. The ‘raise the age’ initiative is proven to decrease crime, increase public safety and improve economic outcomes by allowing emerging adults who are 18 years old—the typical age of a high school senior—to be tried as juveniles instead of adults for certain crimes.

Requiring Automated Criminal Record Sealing (Amendment 511): Automates and expedites the process of sealing criminal records, ensuring that eligible people are able to move forward without bureaucratic delays.

Affordable Homeownership Pilot (Amendment 46): Supports the development and construction of permanently affordable homeownership units by aiding the creation of a pilot program. Authorizes $2.5 million to fund the creation of units for low- and moderate-income households, including units within mixed-use developments.

Municipal Tax Relief (Amendment 554): Gives cities and towns the option of providing enhanced tax relief in the form of a rebate to lower- and middle-income taxpayers who already receive the residential tax exemption. Creates an additional tool on top of the established residential exemption, which gives property tax relief to local residents by shifting more of the residential tax burden onto vacation homes and investment properties.

West-East Passenger Rail (Amendment 196): Authorizes $5 million for the development of the passenger rail station in Palmer, a key stop for West-East Passenger Rail to span the state from Boston to Pittsfield.

The ENOUGH Act (Amendment 401): Creates a fund and framework to capitalize on public-private partnerships to lift families and communities out of poverty. Support would extend to community organizations to boost areas such as early education and care, affordable housing, public safety, and civic infrastructure.

Zoo New England (Amendment 22): Authorizes $5 million for capital improvements at facilities of Zoo New England, which supports education and conservation through the Franklin Park Zoo in Boston and Stone Memorial Zoo in Stoneham.

Massachusetts National Guard Museum Birthplace (Amendment 366): Unlocks federal dollars to support the development of the Massachusetts National Guard Museum by giving an official designation to the museum. Designates the facility’s location as Salem, the birthplace of the National Guard where the first muster of the colonial Militia was held 389 years ago.

The package is based on legislation originally filed by Governor Maura Healey. A prior version was passed by the House of Representatives.

The Senate passed the bill and sent it back to the House of Representatives for further consideration.

news_communities.title: McGonagle Delivers Authentic Copy of Declaration of Independence to Mayor Van Campen, City
news_communities.author: Independent Staff
news_communities.summary:
Special to the Independent

Rep. Joe McGonagle visited Everett City Hall earlier this month to deliver an authentic, handprinted copy of the Declaration of Independence to Mayor Van Campen and the City in honor of the 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration. The Mayor and Representative were joined by McGonagle summer intern and Everett native Emily Buss who is a rising junior at University of Massachusetts Boston.

“I thought this was a fantastic idea to celebrate the 250th anniversary of the signing and bring together the Commonwealth through our different communities,” said McGonagle. “Seeing and reading the Declaration in this format brings to life the magnitude of such a document, what it meant in 1776 and what it means today. I am so grateful to my colleague Rep. Sean Garballey for organizing this venture and thankful for to Mayor Van Campen for all he continues to do for this City.”

The ceremony was part of a push across the Commonwealth for legislators to deliver these documents to each city and town in Massachusetts. The copies come as a result of the efforts of historian and printer Gary Gregory, who has printed hundreds of copies of the Declaration at the Museum of Printing in Haverhill using 18th-century techniques, recreating a labor-intensive process similar to that used in 1776. The effort brings to life a lesser-known chapter of Revolutionary  history, the distribution of the Declaration across all Massachusetts cities and towns just weeks after the Founding Fathers drafted the original document on July 4, 1776.

After its adoption, more than 300 printed copies of the Declaration were sent to parishes throughout the state, where they were read aloud to residents by their ministers, and recorded into official town records. Over one hundred of the original copies remain preserved today, with more still being discovered.

news_communities.title: News in Brief
news_communities.author: Independent Staff
news_communities.summary:
Sheriff Koutoujian applauds Senate move to ban cryptocurrency kiosks

Middlesex Sheriff Peter J. Koutoujian today applauded members of the Massachusetts State Senate for their move to ban cryptocurrency kiosks. Sheriff Koutoujian testified in support of legislation restricting cryptocurrency kiosks in October of last year, and garnered the support of all 14 Massachusetts Sheriffs to ban the machines statewide.

“I am proud to have collaborated closely over the last several months with AARP Massachusetts, my fellow sheriffs and public safety partners, and legislators like Senator John Cronin to push this ban forward because we need to protect residents now and into the future,” said Sheriff Koutoujian. “For far too long, criminals have taken advantage of the unregulated world of cryptocurrency ATMs – or kiosks – to scam people out of their hard-earned savings. We applaud the Massachusetts Senate for supporting a statewide ban on these kiosks to provide much-needed protection to our friends, neighbors and loved ones. We will keep working to see this matter of public policy and public safety become law.”

The language banning the kiosks was included as an amendment on the Senate’s version of the new economic development bill (S3178). The bill is next expected to head to a conference committee to be finalized.

The move to ban the kiosks comes as Massachusetts public safety agencies have repeatedly issued public warnings about the ability of scammers to utilize the machines to defraud unsuspecting residents.  The Middlesex Sheriff’s Office has included warnings in news releases, public service announcements and through community-based presentations over the last two years.

Overnight Closure of Sumner Tunnel

The Massachusetts Department of Transportation (MassDOT) is announcing that the Sumner Tunnel / Route 1A southbound will close to all traffic on Friday, July 31, at 11 p.m. and will reopen to traffic at 6 a.m. the following morning. Travel through the Ted Williams Tunnel (I-90) and Callahan Tunnel (Route 1A northbound) will remain available. A signed detour will be in place during the closure. 

This closure is necessary for crews to safely conduct repairs and maintenance activities.   

Appropriate signage, law enforcement details, and messaging will be in place to guide drivers through the work area.  

Drivers traveling through the affected areas should expect delays, reduce speed, and use caution.   

All scheduled work is weather dependent and subject to change without notice.  

For more information on traffic conditions, travelers are encouraged to:   

• Download the Mass511 mobile app or visit www.mass511.com to view live cameras, travel times, real-time traffic conditions, and project information before setting out on the road. Users can subscribe to receive text and email alerts for traffic conditions.  

• Dial 511 and select a route to hear real-time conditions.     

• Follow @MassDOT on X, (formerly known as Twitter), to receive regular updates on road and traffic conditions.

news_communities.title: DiDomenico Welcomes Sales Tax-free Weekend
news_communities.author: Independent Staff
news_communities.summary:
Special to the Independent

Senator Sal DiDomenico and his colleagues in the Massachusetts Legislature set Saturday, August 8 and Sunday, August 9 as the official dates of Massachusetts’ annual sales tax holiday. During the holiday, the state’s 6.25 percent sales tax will be suspended for most retail items priced under $2,500.  

A 2018 state law, which made the sales tax holiday permanent, requires the Legislature to vote to set the dates of the holiday each year. Both branches adopted resolutions setting this year’s dates (H.5495/S.3119), sponsored by Representative Carole A. Fiola (D-Fall River) and by Senator Nick Collins (D-South Boston). 

“As prices shoot up on all kinds of products thanks to tariffs and foreign wars, this year’s temporary suspension of the sales tax will bring needed relief to consumers while supporting small businesses across the state,” said Senator Sal N. DiDomenico. “I encourage all my residents to take advantage of this weekend, and I look forward to the increased economic activity for stores throughout my district.”

A spike in consumer activity routinely boosts indirect tax revenues. According to the Department of Revenue, the 2025 sales tax holiday generated $3.65 million in indirect tax revenues due to increased economic activity.  

At a time when consumers are seeing prices on store shelves rise, driven in part by federally imposed tariffs, this year’s Massachusetts sales tax holiday will give shoppers a much-needed break. The holiday also encourages families looking to shop for back-to-school season to support local small businesses and retailers.  

Information about eligible purchases is available on the Department of Revenue website.

news_communities.title: Commissioner Rejects Proposed Rate Increase from Fallon Community Health Plan
news_communities.author: Independent Staff
news_communities.summary:
Special to the Independent

Governor Maura Healey announced that the Division of Insurance has negotiated down proposed rate increases from seven health insurers, saving Massachusetts residents and businesses a projected $72 million in health care premiums for 2027.  

The Division of Insurance re-negotiated lower rates with Blue Cross Blue Shield of Massachusetts HMO Blue, INC., Harvard Pilgrim Health Care, Health New England, Mass General Brigham Health Plan, Tufts Health Public Plans, United Healthcare and WellSense Health Plan. These efforts will result in savings for the approximately 670,000 Massachusetts residents and businesses who are enrolled in these plans in the Massachusetts merged market.

Commissioner Michael Caljouw also rejected Fallon Community Health Plan’s proposed 25.7% rate increase for being excessive and inconsistent with his responsibility to Massachusetts consumers and businesses. This disapproval is now subject to an administrative appeal process should the insurance company choose one.

“Massachusetts residents and businesses are already struggling with the high cost of health care. Nobody can afford massive increases in their health insurance premiums on top of that,” said Governor Healey. “Commissioner Caljouw and his team are always looking for ways to lower people’s costs – whether that’s by capping co-pays and deductibles or removing prior authorizations. Now, he’s saving people tens of millions of dollars next year by negotiating with affordability as his focus.”

Last year, Governor Healey signed legislation that increased the Division of Insurance’s consideration of affordability during his review of the merged market rate filings. As a result, Commissioner Caljouw was able to initially save residents and businesses $54 million in 2026 by re-negotiating rate increases. Governor Healey has also taken action to cap health care co-pays and deductibles for the first time in Massachusetts history, and further lowered that cap this year to save people an estimated average of $232 per year. She also eliminated prior authorization requirements for many routine and essential health care services, reducing delays and administrative costs for patients and providers, and prohibited medical debt from appearing on consumer credit reports

news_communities.title: Healey-Driscoll Administration Expands Firefighter Survival Training with New Mobile SCBA Maze
news_communities.author: Independent Staff
news_communities.summary:
Special to the Independent

The Massachusetts Department of Fire Services (DFS) announced the expansion of firefighter survival training at the Massachusetts Firefighting Academy (MFA) with the addition of a new mobile self-contained breathing apparatus (SCBA) training maze. The new training system will increase access to realistic, hands-on instruction for recruit and veteran municipal firefighters across the Commonwealth.

“One of DFS’s most important responsibilities is ensuring firefighters across Massachusetts have access to the highest-quality training possible,” said Public Safety and Security Secretary Gina Kwon. “That means continually investing in modern equipment and training environments that reflect the dangerous and unpredictable conditions firefighters face in the field. Better training builds more confident, better prepared firefighters, and better prepared firefighters help make communities across Massachusetts safer.”

The new mobile training maze expands the MFA’s ability to deliver firefighter survival training both on campus and directly to local fire departments. Combined with the Academy’s existing mobile training resources, it will increase access to realistic, hands-on SCBA training for recruits and experienced firefighters alike. The unit also replaces the Academy’s original Stow-based SCBA maze, ensuring this critical training remains available for years to come.

This year, DFS marks 30 years of training Massachusetts firefighters through the MFA. Since 1996, the Academy has prepared thousands of firefighters for the challenges of the job while continually evolving its training programs to reflect new technologies, emerging hazards, and best practices. The addition of the new mobile SCBA training maze builds on that legacy by giving more firefighters the opportunity to train in realistic, high-pressure environments that build the skills and confidence they need to respond safely and effectively when lives are on the line.

“The SCBA Training Maze is one of our most frequently requested training tools,” said State Fire Marshal Jon M. Davine. “This new mobile unit allows us to deliver critical survival training to more firefighters in more communities while strengthening the MFA’s ability to prepare recruits and veteran firefighters for the dangerous and unpredictable conditions they face. Providing firefighters with realistic training is one of the best investments we can make in their safety and the safety of the communities they serve.”

Inside the maze, firefighters navigate dark, confined, and unfamiliar environments while wearing full turnout gear and SCBA. The training is designed to build confidence under stress, improve air management, and reinforce the skills firefighters rely on during searches, rescues, and self-extrication.

Last year, the MFA’s Springfield-based mobile SCBA maze supported training for more than 500 municipal firefighters. The addition of a second roadworthy mobile unit will expand training opportunities for fire departments across Massachusetts while continuing to support recruit training at the Stow campus.

The new mobile maze is one of several investments that have strengthened training at the MFA in recent years, alongside a forcible entry trailer, flashover training prop, search and rescue buildings on the Bridgewater and Springfield campuses, a hazardous materials leak prop, and a Mobile Extraction Unit used to decontaminate firefighting gear.

DFS invested approximately $500,000 in the new training system, supported in large part by a $435,000 FEMA Assistance to Firefighters Grant. The investment reflects DFS’s continued commitment to providing firefighters across Massachusetts with access to realistic, state-of-the-art training.

news_communities.title: Bar accused of overserving wrong-way driver before deadly crash has hearing
news_communities.author: Robert Goulston, Munashe Kwangwari and Kaitlin McKinley Becker
news_communities.summary:
The bar that served the man whom police say drunkenly drove down the wrong side of Route 1 and killed a Massachusetts state trooper this year is fighting to keep its liquor license.

Operators of Tribu Mexican Kitchen and Bar appeared in front of state alcohol license regulators in Chelsea Tuesday. Hernan Marrero left the restaurant on May 6 two times over the legal driving limit and crashed into Trooper Kevin Trainor’s cruiser, killing them both, prosecutors have said. They didn’t bring charges against Tribu.

Tribu is only allowed to serve alcohol during certain hours and not allowed to let people drink for free. State liquor license regulators testified that the restaurant violated the conditions of their liquor license when they served Marrero nine drinks, seven of them after hours, and didn’t charge him for those drinks.

“A licensee who sells alcohol is quote unquote bound at his own peril to keep within condition of the license,” Henry DiGiacomo, associate general counsel for the Massachusetts Alcoholic Beverages Control Commission.

Tracy Firicano, one of the attorneys representing Tribu, said in her closing statement that the owners have already taken steps to correct their actions.

“They are hard workers. They learn from their experiences. They are responsible owners,” said Firicano. “They seek guidance that will assist them in assimilating any problems they have. They are very willing to take any or all measures to protect their customers.”

Trainor’s mother attended the hearing and later shared a statement that read, in part, “The privilege of holding a liquor license comes with the responsibility to protect the public by refusing to serve visibly intoxicated patrons.”

The commission will make a decision at a later date. Their options are to suspend, revoke or modify the liquor license or take no action at all.

Elijah Garcia delivered an impressive performance at his latest tournament, competing with determination, skill and sportsmanship against some of the best young boxers in the country.

In the opening round, Elijah earned a hard-fought victory over the No. 6-ranked boxer in the nation. The win provided a strong start to the tournament and demonstrated his ability to compete at the highest level.

In the second round, Elijah faced the No. 3-ranked boxer in the country in an extremely competitive bout. After a closely contested match, Elijah fell just short in a split decision.

Although the tournament did not end with the result he had hoped for, Elijah gained valuable experience against elite national competition. His performances have helped establish him as one of the top boxers in his weight class while continuing his development both as an athlete and a young man.

Elijah has already returned to the gym and is training for two major national tournaments later this year.

The USA Boxing National Open will take place in Cleveland, Ohio, from September 26 through October 3. He will then prepare for the USA Boxing National Championships in Lafayette, Louisiana, scheduled for December 5–13.

Each tournament will provide another opportunity for Elijah to test himself against the nation’s best young boxers and continue working toward his goals in the sport.

news_communities.title: City moves ahead with 9 Chelsea Street project slated for 120 units
news_communities.author: admin
news_communities.summary:
BPDA approves project that completed two public meetings earlier in the process; site of the former Rapino Funeral Home. Development long in the waiting.

The Boston Planning & Development Agency has approved a six-story, 120-unit mixed-use development at 9 Chelsea Street, a long-vacant property at the edge of Maverick Square in East Boston.

The BPDA Board approved the project on July 16, allowing the development to advance through the remaining design, permitting and compliance stages of the city’s Article 80 review process. The approximately 84,267-square-foot building will include rental housing, affordable units, ground-floor retail space and extensive improvements to the surrounding sidewalks and public realm.

March meeting highlighted community concerns

Residents and nearby stakeholders raised several concerns about the proposed development, particularly its scale and impact on the character of Maverick Square. Some residents argued that the six-story building remains too tall and imposing compared with surrounding structures and could significantly change the character of the square and adjoining neighborhood. Although the project has undergone revisions, critics continued to question whether its overall size and massing are appropriate for the site.

Parking and traffic were also major concerns. Residents pointed to an existing shortage of neighborhood parking and congestion that can become particularly difficult during snow emergencies and periods of construction. The impact of parking associated with the East Boston Neighborhood Health Center (now NeighborHealth) was also cited. Some residents questioned the project’s reliance on transit access as a reason for providing no off-street parking, arguing that even if only a portion of the building’s tenants own vehicles, the addition could place further pressure on neighborhood streets. Because residents of the development would be eligible for neighborhood parking permits, critics expressed skepticism that proximity to Maverick Station would necessarily translate into a largely car-free tenant population.

The proposed mix of apartments generated additional discussion, particularly the large number of studios and other smaller units. Residents argued that such a mix could appeal primarily to young professionals or students rather than families and questioned whether the development does enough to provide family-sized housing in a neighborhood already facing concerns about displacement. Some also raised the possibility that studio apartments could eventually be used for short-term rentals such as Airbnb. The development team responded that short-term rentals are subject to separate city regulations, zoning and registration requirements and said operating the building as short-term accommodations is not part of its business model.

The amount and type of ground-floor retail also drew criticism. Several residents said a prominent site of approximately 18,802 square feet at Maverick Square should accommodate more substantial commercial space, potentially including a grocery store or supermarket, rather than primarily smaller businesses such as cafés, salons or similar establishments.

The development team said it had tested demand with major retail brokers and contacted approximately 37 prospective tenants, including national retailers, but found little interest in a large-format location at the site. Based on that outreach, the developer concluded that smaller storefronts designed for walkable, neighborhood-serving businesses represented a more financially viable and leasable approach.

The project, proposed by 9 Chelsea Street LLC, affiliated with DND Homes, will be constructed on approximately 18,975 square feet of vacant land at Chelsea and Maverick streets.

120 Apartments Planned Near Maverick Square

Plans call for 120 rental apartments consisting of 76 studios, 25 one-bedroom units and 19 two-bedroom units.

The building will also contain approximately 5,492 square feet of ground-floor retail space divided between two commercial units. Plans include approximately 802 square feet of ground-floor amenity space, a 3,568-square-foot common roof deck and 2,254 square feet of at-grade open space.

The development is located approximately 500 feet from Maverick Station on the MBTA Blue Line and is also served by nearby bus routes and seasonal East Boston ferry service.

22 Affordable and Voucher Units

Twenty-two of the building’s apartments will be income-restricted or reserved for households using mobile housing vouchers.

Eighteen units will be income-restricted at an average of 60 percent of Area Median Income. Of those, five will be available to households earning no more than 50 percent of AMI, eight at no more than 60 percent of AMI and five at no more than 70 percent of AMI.

Another four units will be made available to households using mobile housing vouchers.

The affordable and voucher units must be distributed throughout the development and comparable in design and quality to the market-rate apartments. Affordability restrictions may remain in effect for as long as 50 years.

The project also completed the city’s Affirmatively Furthering Fair Housing review. Commitments include placing all Inclusionary Zoning units on site, providing more accessible units than required, increasing the proportion of larger income-restricted units and adopting inclusive tenant-screening and marketing practices.

No Automobile Parking Planned

Despite a project metrics table listing a maximum parking allowance, the proposal itself includes no automobile parking. Instead, the project emphasizes its proximity to public transportation and bicycle facilities.

Approximately 150 bicycle spaces are planned, including long-term storage for residents and short-term bicycle parking around the building.

The developer will also contribute $49,000 toward Boston’s bikeshare program and provide space nearby for a 15-dock bikeshare station.

Sidewalk and Maverick Square Improvements

The project includes reconstruction and widening of sidewalks along Chelsea, Maverick and Bremen streets.

Improvements will include accessible pedestrian zones, permeable furnishing areas, new street trees, bicycle racks, upgraded curb ramps and improved street lighting where necessary.

Curbside regulations along Maverick Street are also expected to be modified during daytime hours to provide space for short-term pickups, rideshare vehicles and deliveries.

The developer has agreed to contribute $100,307 toward public-realm and transportation improvements identified through the Maverick Square Transportation Action Plan.

Additional community contributions include $17,000 to East Boston Main Streets to support local small businesses and $17,000 to Tree Eastie to help expand the neighborhood’s tree canopy.

Project Designed Around Transit and PLAN: East Boston

The property is located within East Boston’s Mixed-Use-7 zoning district and falls within the area covered by PLAN: East Boston, the neighborhood planning initiative adopted by the BPDA Board in January 2024 and incorporated into zoning later that year.

The city’s plan encourages additional housing and mixed-use development around East Boston’s major squares and transit stations while calling for active ground-floor uses.

Planning staff concluded that the Chelsea Street proposal is consistent with those goals. Retail entrances will face Maverick Square, while the residential entrance will be oriented toward the adjoining residential area.

The developer requires zoning relief for lot coverage, side yards and a rear stepback. Planning officials attributed those requests largely to the irregular configuration of the property.

All-Electric, Passive House Design

The building is being designed as an all-electric development using heat pumps for space conditioning and hot water, energy-recovery ventilation, an airtight and highly insulated building envelope and Energy Star-rated appliances.

The project is expected to meet Passive House certification requirements and is designed to be certifiable at the LEED Gold level.

It will also be solar-ready and is registered for the Mass Save Passive House Incentive Program. The developer has committed to purchasing 100 percent renewable electricity for common building loads.

Plans also incorporate stormwater infiltration, green infrastructure, smart streetlights and broadband infrastructure as part of Boston’s Smart Utilities requirements.

Project Advances Following Article 80 Review

The developer filed its Project Notification Form in February. Public review included an Impact Advisory Group meeting on March 10, a public meeting on March 11 and another Impact Advisory Group meeting on May 28.

Community feedback led to changes including increased ground-floor retail, provisions for deliveries and rideshare activity and modifications to the building’s massing and layout.

State Rep. Adrian Madaro submitted a letter supporting the development, citing its housing, affordable housing, transit-oriented location and alignment with PLAN: East Boston.

With the BPDA Board’s approval, the agency’s director is authorized to waive further Article 80 review and issue certifications of compliance once remaining requirements are satisfied. Design review will continue as the developer works toward final construction documents and permitting.

news_communities.title: Maverick Landing Community Services launches Grab & Go produce market, expanding affordable fresh food access across East Boston
news_communities.author: admin
news_communities.summary:
EAST BOSTON, MA — Maverick Landing Community Services (MLCS) officially celebrated the opening of its new Grab & Go Produce Market on July 23, Thursday bringing together more than 70 residents, elected officials, community partners, funders, and volunteers to mark a major milestone in expanding affordable fresh food access and economic opportunity for East Boston families.

The new Grab & Go Produce Market offers a simple, dignified way for residents to access affordable fresh produce and artisan bread while connecting them to a broader network of support services, including housing stability, English classes, workforce development, financial education, and digital literacy.

The celebration featured remarks from Executive Director Rita Lara, State Representative Adrian Madaro, Victor Pelatere from Senator Lydia Edwards’ office, and Gabriella Ramirez from Boston City Councilor Gabriela “Gigi” Coletta Zapata’s office, followed by a citation presentation, a family testimonial, lunch, and guided tours of the new market.

In her remarks, Lara reflected on how the initiative grew from the community’s response during the COVID-19 pandemic. “Six years ago, the pandemic exposed just how fragile food access could be. What began as an emergency response with Fair Foods has grown into a long-term commitment to ensuring every family has access to healthy food with dignity.”

During the pandemic, MLCS partnered with Fair Foods, a 38-year produce rescue organization, to launch four weekly produce markets serving East Boston residents. In 2020 alone, the partnership distributed more than 500,000 pounds of fresh produce throughout the neighborhood.

Since then, MLCS has continued expanding its food access efforts. 

Over the past five years, the organization has distributed more than 1.2 million pounds of healthy food in East Boston. Through its expanded regional food rescue operations, MLCS now expects to rescue and distribute more than 1.2 million pounds of fresh produce and artisan bread annually across Greater Boston.

The Grab & Go Produce Market also represents the next chapter in MLCS’s partnership with Fair Foods. As Fair Foods transitions its leadership after nearly four decades of serving Greater Boston, MLCS is helping preserve and strengthen the organization’s legacy by expanding affordable food distribution throughout the region.

Unlike traditional food distribution models, Grab & Go allows residents to place orders in advance by text or online and pick up their food at a convenient time, reducing wait times and creating a more private, welcoming experience for families. All are welcome! Community residents can sign up for Grab & Go at mlcsboston.org. 

“This model recognizes that people’s lives are busy and that everyone deserves convenient, respectful access to healthy food,” Lara said. “There are no long lines, no unnecessary barriers—just fresh food and a community that cares.”

The new market is also designed as a flexible community space. Throughout the week, it will serve as a classroom for English language learners, host workforce and job readiness activities, provide digital skills support, and offer arts and community programming.

MLCS estimates that families using the Grab & Go Produce Market can save approximately $5,000 to $7,000 annually on grocery expenses, helping reduce financial pressure while improving access to healthy food.

“Today’s celebration is about much more than opening a market,” Lara said. “It reflects our commitment to listening to our community and building practical, innovative solutions that help people thrive. We hope every resident who walks through these doors finds not only fresh food, but also new opportunities and the support they need to build a stronger future.”

About Maverick Landing Community Services

Founded in 2007, Maverick Landing Community Services (MLCS) is a nonprofit community organization serving East Boston residents by building pathways to stability and opportunity. MLCS provides affordable food access, housing stability services, workforce development, adult education, youth programming, financial education, digital literacy, and community health initiatives. With its food expansion MLCS is serving over 5000 residents per year across Greater Boston and is expected to rescue over 1M lbs of produce in 2026.
